articles.title: Pentagon probes how China got parts for F-35s
articles.body:
The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the US’ most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet on Wednesday reporting that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the US Department of Defense are aware of “a shipment issue” with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Photo: AP
UPS was shipping a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door from an Australian military F-35 that was being sent to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal in late May, said people briefed on the incident, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
Both parts, supplied by Lockheed Martin Corp, were coated with radar-absorbing material that enhances their stealth capabilities, two of the people said.
The plane stopped in South Korea en route to the US and from there it was routed to Hong Kong, one of the people said.
It is not clear why the plane stopped in South Korea or why it was diverted to Hong Kong, or whether the parts were intentionally diverted or by mistake.
The Chinese government later took possession of the parts, and has not returned them, two of the people said.
Australian Minister for Defence Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred,” he said.
A Chinese embassy spokesman declined immediate comment, while the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday said it was “not aware of the situation.”
Disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries. Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) arrived in the US on Wednesday evening for a state visit hosted by US President Donald Trump.
At least two congressional committees are investigating how the parts fell into Chinese hands.
China’s possession of the parts, the stop in South Korea and the fact that UPS was used to transport them had not been previously reported. Politico reported earlier that the parts had been unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
“The juxtaposition is hard to miss,” US Senator Elissa Slotkin said on Bloomberg Television’s Balance of Power. “The Chinese are holding some of our most sensitive technology and we are rolling out the red carpet for their president.”
Slotkin said she had not received a briefing on the issue.
“When it comes to intelligence and military issues, China is a competitor and an adversary. They are always seeking information about our military equipment, sensitive information,” she said.
China has for years targeted the F-35 in its espionage efforts. Concerns that China could learn valuable intelligence about the jet were one reason why a US bid to sell F-35s to the United Arab Emirates, announced in Trump’s first term, later collapsed.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” said Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington-based think tank.
Bowman in November last year said that US military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35’s technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
The plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat, Bowman said.
The Pentagon said it was working to retrieve the parts.
Officials “are aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 components. We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” it said in a statement.
A Lockheed Martin spokesperson in Australia yesterday said in a statement that “the components in question are unserviceable and deemed low risk for exploitation.”
“It’s always best when your adversaries have to guess at your capabilities,” said J.J. Gertler, a former aviation analyst for Congressional Research Service who is now director of The Defense Concepts Organization. “You never want to hand them evidence.”
UPS disclosed the incident to the US Department of State’s Directorate of Defense Trade Controls, which enforces export control laws, out of an abundance of caution. Company spokesman Malcolm Berkley declined to comment.
During a closed US Senate Committee on Armed Services F-35 hearing on June 23, defense department program office officials expressed their hope the components would be returned, people familiar with the exchange said.
The diversion is being reviewed by two House congressional panels — House Foreign Affairs and Armed Services committees.
House Armed Services Committee spokeswoman Heather Vaughan said the “committee is aware of this issue and we’ve received multiple briefings on it.”
The Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Airland also “is aware of the reports and is currently looking into the matter,” spokesman Dave Vasquez said.

The US military came close to boarding a Chinese vessel in the Middle East earlier this year based on a flawed intelligence report prepared with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), CNN said on Friday. US intelligence indicated the ship was carrying nuclear weapons-related components, leading US forces to prepare to intercept it, the broadcaster reported, citing four anonymous sources familiar with the incident. However, the operation was called off after officials determined that an AI chatbot used by an analyst had misidentified the material the ship was carrying. The report was “entirely false,” but “almost started a war,” CNN quoted one source
World leaders gather in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, bracing for US President Donald Trump’s return to the rostrum for a second year running, with talks centering on the widening conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and the risks of artificial intelligence (AI). Nearly 130 heads of state meet with the post-World War II order under strain and with the UN itself struggling to remain relevant and weathering attacks from Trump, who has slashed the US’ contributions and withdrawn from dozens of UN bodies. Typhoon Dujuan forced the cancellation of at least 275 flights in Japan today and prompted warnings of potentially record-breaking rainfall as the storm nears Tokyo. The typhoon, which is accompanied by high winds, has also led to the early closure in Tokyo of one the world’s biggest video game trade fairs and knocked out power for thousands. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) warned yesterday that rain and winds were expected to intensify even before the typhoon’s arrival. “The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain,” the agency said. articles.title: PET warns of increased Russian espionage and sabotage in Denmark
articles.body:
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.
This applies both to physical security and cybersecurity, according to Rasmus Anderskouv, DI’s deputy director for societal security and emergency preparedness.
“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.
DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.

Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.
The second phase will focus on Danish and Nordic art from 1750 to 1900. Among the works to be displayed is August Jerndorff’s “Portrait of Marie Oppermann” from 1894.
The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.
At the same time, Løkke said the agreement contains “no financing elements”.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that an agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland was being reached without costs for the United States.
“There will be no cost to the US,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, with the words “no cost” written in capital letters.
Asked how that could be the case if the US will finance new bases, Løkke said:
“You’ll have to ask him about that.”
“But it is not as though they have to pay ground rent,” he added.
Løkke said the “further terms” for the two new US military bases in Greenland still need to be agreed upon.
The bases must also take the environment and Greenlandic lifestyle and culture into account, he said.
“These are important things that strengthen Greenland in relation to the 1951 agreement,” Løkke said.
He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.
“That is, after all, completely obvious,” he said.
Pituffik Space Base was previously known as Thule Air Base and has around 150 US military personnel stationed there.
Under the new security and defense agreement, the US has been granted permission to establish new bases in the settlement of Narsarsuaq and in Mestersvig.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a written response that the new agreement between the three countries “does not concern financing”.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.
American singer and actress Hilary Duff will perform in Denmark next year as she expands her upcoming tour with 32 additional concerts.
The 38-year-old will play at Royal Arena in Copenhagen on May 20, 2027.
The additional concerts follow strong demand across several countries and will take Duff’s ‘Lucky Me’ tour through Europe, Latin America and the U.S.
The newly announced part of the tour begins in Madrid on May 7, 2027. Duff is also scheduled to perform in cities including Berlin, Amsterdam, Paris and Stockholm.
General ticket sales begin Friday, October 2, 2026.
Duff became widely known as a child actor through the Disney series Lizzie McGuire, which ran from 2001 to 2004. She also appeared in the 2003 film of the same name.
In 2003, Duff released the album Metamorphosis, which included the song ‘Come Clean.’ She is also behind ‘What Dreams Are Made Of’ from the same year.
Duff later appeared in films including A Cinderella Story and The Perfect Man.
Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.
“When more children in the world’s poorest countries go to school and learn to read and do math, it creates fertile ground for economic growth and new markets for Danish business,” he said.
The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
A young man was stabbed with a knife at Brøndbyøster Station on Wednesday.
A young man was stabbed with a knife at Brøndbyøster Station on Wednesday, Copenhagen West Police said on Politi Update.
The man was taken to Rigshospitalet for treatment. Police said they could not immediately provide information about his condition.
Police have arrested a suspect in connection with the stabbing.
Copenhagen West Police’s press unit told Ritzau shortly before 4 p.m. that it would not provide further information about the case at that time.
Police were still working at the scene Wednesday afternoon. S-trains were running but were not stopping at Brøndbyøster Station, according to DSB’s website.
According to Ekstra Bladet, the area around the station was cordoned off and several patrol cars were at the scene. The newspaper also reported that an ambulance had been seen leaving from the northern side of the station.
The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.
Stena Line has ordered two new hybrid ferries for the route between Frederikshavn and Gothenburg, with the vessels expected to enter service in 2030.
The company announced the order in a press release Wednesday.
The ferries will be built at a shipyard in China. They will be E-Flexer vessels with room for 1,500 passengers.
The hybrid ferries will run on both electricity and conventional fuel. They are expected to continue doing so until charging options allow them to operate fully on electricity.
“It is a historic investment for Stena Line, which gives us the opportunity to take another step in the sustainable modernization of our fleet,” Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line, said.
“They support our goal of reducing CO₂ emissions and preparing the fleet for future environmental requirements,” he said.
Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.
Nationalbank expects Danish economy to grow 4% this year
Denmark’s economy is expected to grow 4% this year, according to a new forecast from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank. The forecast marks a sharp increase from the central bank’s previous projection in March, when it expected gross domestic product, or GDP, to grow 1.8% this year. There appears to be broad political support in Denmark for a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States.
The agreement, signed Tuesday in New York by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump, must now go through approval procedures in Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut, and the Folketing, Denmark’s national parliament.
The agreement is intended to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The signing took place at the United Nations headquarters during the U.N. General Assembly.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a desire for the United States to own Greenland, citing national and international security concerns. His statements led to a prolonged diplomatic crisis between the United States, Denmark and Greenland.
Several Danish political parties have welcomed the agreement, including Venstre, the Conservative Party, the Red-Green Alliance and the Denmark Democrats.
Venstre’s chairman, Troels Lund Poulsen, described the agreement as “an extraordinarily good agreement.”
Poulsen was defense minister in the former SVM government, a coalition between the Social Democrats, Venstre and the Moderates, and played a significant role in the negotiations with the Trump administration.
“It is a joyful day for Greenland, Denmark, the Realm, and for the cooperation with the USA in the future,” he told TV 2 on Tuesday.
When Frederiksen held a press conference for Danish media in New York, she gave particular thanks to Poulsen for his efforts. Poulsen described it as “beautiful” that the agreement had become a reality.
The Conservative Party’s chairman, Mona Juul, also praised the agreement on Facebook.
“An agreement has been reached. And that is unequivocally good. Therefore, I would also like to praise the enormous political and diplomatic work that preceded the agreement,” she wrote.
The Denmark Democrats’ chairman, Inger Støjberg, also expressed support.
“It is an agreement we can be proud of, because it both emphasizes our sovereignty and cements NATO’s presence,” she told TV 2 on Tuesday, referring to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The Red-Green Alliance, a party that supports the government in parliament, also backed the agreement.
“It is an agreement that does not in any way alter Danish sovereignty. An agreement that Greenland signs with Denmark and the USA. They have stayed within the red lines,” the party’s Greenland spokesperson, Trine Pertou Mach, told Jyllands-Posten on Tuesday.
The agreement will enter into force only after the necessary parliamentary procedures have been completed.

Small public schools in rural areas are set to receive more state support as falling numbers of children put some schools at risk of closing.
The government is allocating 500 million DKK through 2030 to support small schools and slow further closures.
Minister for Economic and Interior Affairs Pia Olsen Dyhr from the Socialist People’s Party, is presenting the plan today at a visit to a school in Toksværd in Næstved Municipality, according to TV2 ØST.
“A school is a gathering point for parents, teachers, and students, and they help create local life and connection in our rural districts,” Dyhr said.
The initiative follows a commitment in the government’s platform from June to prevent a new wave of school closures. Small public schools in rural areas are also expected to receive greater financial support and more freedom.
One school facing possible closure is Vesterlandsskolen’s branch in Hyllinge. Only fifty-four students attend this school, and Næstved Municipality’s administration has proposed ending teaching and after-school care there from August 1, 2027.
Closing the branch would save 7.53 million DKK annually from 2028. The proposal has not been approved, and the city council is expected to adopt its budget on October 6.
School board chair Karina Wolan said additional state funding could help keep the Hyllinge branch open.
“If it means that the school can be allowed to exist, that would be wonderful,” she said.
It remains unclear how the 500 million DKK will be distributed, which municipalities will qualify and whether the funding is included in the government’s previously announced five billion DKK annual investment in children, daycare, schools and leisure.
Social Affairs Minister Monika Rubin of the Moderates says the government wants more freedom to change Denmark’s disability system after withdrawing from a political agreement reached two years ago.
The framework agreement was signed in May 2024 by the government and Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and the Social Liberal Party. It was not a formal political settlement with special rules governing withdrawal.
“With the framework agreement, one had bound oneself in a way that made it more difficult than it needs to be to cooperate broadly across the Folketing,” Rubin said, referring to Denmark’s parliament.
“The original agreement has outlived its potential,” she added.
When the deal was reached, then-Social Affairs Minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil of the Social Democrats described it as a “completely new chapter in Danish disability policy” and the “first major agreement in the disability area ever.”
Rubin’s Moderates also supported the agreement at the time.
Rubin now says she will work on initiatives involving “fundamental changes to the disability area,” with more trust, structure and coordination of professional expertise around people with disabilities.
The decision drew different responses from other parties.
Katrine Daugaard, social affairs spokesperson for Liberal Alliance, a Danish liberal party, accused Rubin of “running away from an agreement.” She said ending it risks “more uniform, mediocre public services, less specialization, and less freedom of choice.”
Torsten Gejl, political spokesperson for the Alternative, a Danish green party that was not part of the agreement, welcomed the decision.
“The framework agreement for disability, which has tightened the finances in the disability area and made people with disabilities feel like a cost-cutting exercise, was suddenly dropped this evening. That is fantastic,” Gejl wrote on X.
Queen Mary and Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization Christina Egelund will present the Teaching Prize 2026 to teachers from seven higher education institutions.
The award recognizes educators for inspiring and engaging students, the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization said in a press release.
Each recipient receives 500,000 DKK. Of that amount, 200,000 DKK is a personal award, while 300,000 DKK must be used to develop new teaching activities.
The awards will be presented at the Opera in Copenhagen.
“For this year’s seven prize recipients, good teaching is about awakening the students’ curiosity and creating engagement,” Egelund, from the Moderates, said.
She added that the recipients had also created learning environments where students felt comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.
The seven recipients come from different areas of higher education.
Assistant Professor Amalie Trangbæk teaches political science at Aarhus University. Assistant Lecturer Brian Jørgensen teaches communication design at Design School Kolding, while Associate Professor Bjarne Schmidt teaches mathematics, physics and engineering didactics at the University of Southern Denmark.
The other recipients are Associate Professor Lars Plauborg Pedersen from Syddansk Erhvervsakademi, Associate Professor René Kirk Johansen from the maritime and polytechnic education center Martec, Associate Professor Gry Segoli from Københavns Professionshøjskole and Associate Professor Lene Krogstrup Jakobsen from UC SYD in Esbjerg.
Educational institutions nominate candidates for the prize each year. Relevant groups of rectors then assess the nominations and decide which candidates are put forward to the Minister for Research, Education and Digitalization.
Several Danish newspapers said Wednesday that Denmark and Greenland welcomed the new security and defense agreement, even as they raised questions about its consequences.
Berlingske called the deal a “triumph for wise and persistent diplomacy” in an editorial.
“If the agreement turns out to be worth the paper it is written on, foreign policy history was written in New York on Tuesday,” the newspaper wrote.
Politiken described the agreement signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen and U.S. President Donald Trump as a “diplomatic masterpiece.”
Politiken said the deal protects Greenland’s territorial integrity, but also described it as a high-risk agreement whose details remain open to interpretation.
Kristeligt Dagblad called it a “historic agreement on the security of the Kingdom of Denmark’s Arctic area” and said the Danish government could be satisfied with the result.
Other newspapers focused more strongly on the risks.
Ekstra Bladet described the agreement as a costly victory. It raised concerns that the U.S. could use Greenland for activities unrelated to NATO, including establishing its “Golden Dome” missile defense system there.
“We are paying a high, but unavoidable price,” Ekstra Bladet wrote. “We can well call it a victory, as long as we remember how dearly it was bought.”
Information described the agreement as a victory for the Kingdom of Denmark but also as a “submission to a tyrannical superior power.”
Despite its positive assessment of the agreement, Berlingske also warned that uncertainty remains because Trump is president.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.
More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.
Shares in several companies operating in Greenland rose sharply after reports that Denmark, Greenland and the United States are close to an agreement concerning the Arctic territory, TV 2 reports.
Greenland Energy, which extracts oil and gas, rose 135 percent in US trading. Greenland Mines gained 148 percent.
Both companies had lost more than 80 percent of their market value before Monday’s increases.
Critical Metals Corp., which extracts rare earth minerals in Greenland, rose 34 percent.
The increases followed indications that Greenland, Denmark and the United States had reached or were close to reaching an agreement. Its details have not been made public.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates have traveled to the United States.
They are expected to take part in the signing of an agreement involving Denmark, Greenland and the United States during the week.
The three governments have said the planned agreement is intended to strengthen security cooperation in Greenland, the Arctic and the North Atlantic.
Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.

A 31-year-old man has been charged with assault after a Swedish man was punched during a World Cup viewing event at Islands Brygge in Copenhagen on 30 June.
The Swedish man, who was 32, died three days later, on 3 July, according to the Copenhagen Police prosecution service.
The 31-year-old has been charged under section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers ordinary assault.
According to prosecutors, the man struck the Swedish man with a powerful punch from a clenched fist to the left side of his head or neck.
The blow caused, among other injuries, a rupture of an artery, which led to the Swedish man’s death.
The 31-year-old is also charged with throwing two beer cans toward a group of people that included the Swedish man. Another person was hit by one of the cans.
Because the accused has previously been convicted of assault, the case also includes section 247 of the Penal Code. Under that provision, a sentence can be increased by up to half.
The prosecutor in the case has previously said the 31-year-old faces a prison sentence of between eight and 10 months.
That is considerably shorter than a sentence under section 245, which covers aggravated assault and can also apply when a victim dies as a result of an assault.
In this case, prosecutors have charged the man only under the ordinary assault provision.
Criminal law expert Lotte Helms, an assistant professor at the University of Southern Denmark, previously explained to Ritzau that a single punch with a fist will normally fall under section 244.
“A punch with a fist will as a starting point be 244, but I cannot rule out that it could fall under 245 if, for example, one has specifically gone after hitting the neck in a specific way,” she said in July.
“But it will always be a specific and individual assessment, and in the end it is the courts that assess it,” she said.
The 31-year-old is a Danish citizen. During an earlier court hearing, he said he came to Denmark from Congo when he was four months old.
The case will be heard at the Copenhagen City Court on 7 October.
Denmark could face more Russian espionage, influence operations and sabotage if Russia intensifies its hybrid war, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, PET, says.
The warning comes in a press release Thursday, following a new threat assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
PET says the expected increase concerns both the scope and nature of Russian espionage, influence and sabotage.
In Denmark, PET has observed “an increased Russian willingness to take risks and concrete planning and preparation of sabotage”, according to the assessment.
The threat of increased sabotage is particularly directed at companies in the defense industry and other organizations with a direct connection to military support for Ukraine.
The warning also applies to possible sabotage and increased espionage targeting what PET describes as “critical infrastructure and other functions vital to society”.
PET, which handles Denmark’s domestic security, says the threat picture has become more “serious and complex”.
PET does not provide details about specific countermeasures. The intelligence service says, however, that it “together with the police is implementing the necessary security measures”.
Dansk Industri, DI, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, says companies need to pay attention to their security.
This applies both to physical security and cybersecurity, according to Rasmus Anderskouv, DI’s deputy director for societal security and emergency preparedness.
“Hybrid attacks against Denmark and Danish companies are unfortunately a new normal that we have to relate to,” he said in a press release.
DI describes the situation as serious and calls for closer cooperation between public authorities and the business sector.
Statens Museum for Kunst, Denmark’s national gallery in Copenhagen, is planning an “ambitious transformation project” aimed at making its collection accessible to more people.
The museum, known as SMK, said the project will include renovations and an “architectural rethinking” of its building on Sølvgade, which opened in 1896.
The project is financed by foundation donations totaling 70.5 million kroner. This includes 15 million kroner from Den A.P. Møllerske Støttefond and 8 million kroner from Ny Carlsbergfondet.
The renovation will respect the original architecture and existing buildings, according to SMK.
It will allow the museum to display more of its approximately 200,000 works. SMK plans to bring artworks back from castles and ministries, along with works that have rarely or never been shown at the museum.
The first phase of the new collection exhibitions will focus on European art from the 1300s to the 1800s.
About half of the works displayed in this section will have never or rarely been shown at SMK. They will include “Susanna in the Bath” by Dutch artist Godefridus Schalcken.
“We want to create a museum where more people experience that art concerns them, and that the collection is something they have a share in,” director Astrid la Cour said.
The project will also focus on helping visitors find their way through the museum, improving physical accessibility and highlighting the historical qualities of the original museum building, designed by architect Vilhelm Dahlerup.
The new exhibitions will open in stages between 2027 and 2029.
Each stage will focus on one of the museum’s three main collection areas: European art, Danish and Nordic art, and Danish and international art.

The United States will pay for any new American military bases established in Greenland under a new security and defense agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen says.
“To the extent that the Americans are to build American bases in Greenland, that is of course something that the Americans finance,” Løkke told Ritzau.
At the same time, Løkke said the agreement contains “no financing elements”.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that an agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland was being reached without costs for the United States.
“There will be no cost to the US,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, with the words “no cost” written in capital letters.
Asked how that could be the case if the US will finance new bases, Løkke said:
“You’ll have to ask him about that.”
“But it is not as though they have to pay ground rent,” he added.
Løkke said the “further terms” for the two new US military bases in Greenland still need to be agreed upon.
The bases must also take the environment and Greenlandic lifestyle and culture into account, he said.
“These are important things that strengthen Greenland in relation to the 1951 agreement,” Løkke said.
He also emphasized that the US pays for improvements at Pituffik Space Base, the only US military base currently in Greenland.
“That is, after all, completely obvious,” he said.
Pituffik Space Base was previously known as Thule Air Base and has around 150 US military personnel stationed there.
Under the new security and defense agreement, the US has been granted permission to establish new bases in the settlement of Narsarsuaq and in Mestersvig.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a written response that the new agreement between the three countries “does not concern financing”.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months, with attacks becoming more frequent and potentially having greater consequences for affected countries, according to a new assessment from the Danish Defence Intelligence Service, FE.
The assessment is being presented Thursday at a press conference at Kastellet in Copenhagen.
FE says the increased threat could include destructive cyberattacks with serious consequences for critical societal functions, as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus, a member of the Social Democrats, said the situation was serious.
“The situation is serious, and we take it seriously,” Bruus said.
“That is why we are standing here today. We are presenting the assessment because having as much openness as possible is important,” he said.
FE also assesses that there is a “low, but increasing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
“It is unlikely that Russia will initiate an actual invasion of a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out,” FE chief Thomas Ahrenkiel said.
Ahrenkiel said it was new that FE could no longer rule out such an invasion.
According to the assessment, Russia would need at least six months to prepare for an actual invasion of a NATO country.
Bruus stressed that the assessment does not concern a possible military attack on Denmark.
“One is not talking about military attacks on the Kingdom of Denmark” in the assessment, he said.
Chief of Defence Michael Hyldgaard, who also attended the press conference, said the Danish military is adapting to the assessment.
“We will fight and win with what we have, and those we fight alongside. That is our task. That is what we are preparing for. We are ready for that – regardless of the threat,” Hyldgaard said.
The assessment does not concern Greenland or the Faroe Islands, according to the information presented at the press conference.
The new assessment comes just over a week after a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish helicopter in international waters off Gedser.
Ahrenkiel described the incident as “unprofessional behavior” by Russian soldiers aboard the frigate.
“It is also our impression that such risky behavior was not sanctioned by the Russian military leadership,” he said.
People in Italy can expect around 11 more years without health-related limitations than people in Denmark, according to figures from the EU’s statistical office, Eurostat.
The figures cover healthy life years across the 27 EU countries. Danes have 62.4 healthy life years, while Italy ranks highest at 73.4.
Healthy life years measure the number of years a person can expect to live without limitations in daily life because of health. Eurostat’s indicator is based on people’s own assessment of their health.
Denmark ranks below 18 other countries in the figures.
Neighboring Sweden and Norway also rank above Denmark, with 67.5 and 64.8 healthy life years respectively.
Diabetes Association calls for greater focus on prevention
The Diabetes Association has described the Danish figures as a “health alarm.”
“Because the figures show that we in Denmark have dragged our feet for too long when it comes to health promotion and preventing chronic illnesses such as type 2 diabetes, which is growing explosively,” the association’s CEO, Claus Richter, said in a press release.
The Eurostat figures cover 2024. It is the first year in which Denmark’s figures have been calculated using the same method as the rest of the EU.
Life expectancy in Denmark has increased year by year. But Richter said the figures show that Danes are living longer “but not better.”
He attributed this in part to a health care system that prioritizes treatment over health promotion and prevention.
He also pointed to what he described as an outdated financial silo mentality, in which an expense in one area “can rarely be justified” by gains in another.
“It is a tragedy for each individual, but also for our society. Illness pulls many thousands of full-time equivalent jobs out of the workforce. Therefore, there is a need for a paradigm shift where we view prevention and health promotion as an investment – not an expense,” he said.
The Diabetes Association is proposing that Denmark set a national target for healthy life years in legislation.
Its vision for 2045 is for Denmark to be among the European countries with the highest number of healthy life years.
Among its proposals is the creation of a Health Economics Council that would assess and prioritize preventive measures based on their long-term value.
The Diabetes Association is due to present the proposal Thursday morning at a health policy debate at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketinget.
Denmark’s wolf population has grown to 77, an increase of 28 from the previous monitoring year, according to a new count by Aarhus University and the Natural History Museum Aarhus.
The figures are included in a memo from the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment.
The population is approaching a size at which it may become possible to regulate the predator, Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said in comments to DR and TV 2.
The ministry will now count the wolves individually. It expects that the results will allow Denmark to “demonstrate to the EU that the wolf has a favorable conservation status.”
“Then we can begin hunting, and we should,” Rabjerg Madsen told DR.
According to the Danish Nature Agency, a species has a favorable conservation status when its population development shows that it can maintain itself in the long term.
Wolves have been protected under the EU Habitats Directive since 1992. The directive “prohibits deliberate killing.”
In Denmark, the protection is implemented through the Hunting and Game Management Act, which prohibits hunting or capturing wolves. Shooting a wolf can result in a fine or imprisonment for up to two years.
However, the Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment can grant permission to regulate, meaning shoot, an individual wolf in special circumstances.
The authorities can grant permission if there is no other solution and the action does not threaten the wolf’s natural range.
This can include cases involving “public health, safety, and security, or to prevent serious damage to livestock and other forms of property.”
An exemption can also be granted if a wolf “lacks an instinctive shyness towards humans.”
The 77 wolves are spread across 11 packs, which have produced a total of 61 pups this year. There are also two pairs of wolves and two lone male wolves in Denmark.
They have been identified in at least 15 locations, all in Jutland, from Løgumkloster in Southern Jutland to the northernmost part of Northern Jutland.
Wolves may also be present in three additional locations, but further investigations are needed to confirm this.
Without “human persecution,” the Danish wolf population is expected to continue growing.
The wolf returned to Denmark from Germany in 2012 after being absent from the country for almost 200 years.
A new resident has arrived among the leopards at Copenhagen Zoo after an Amur leopard gave birth to a cub last week.
The zoo announced the birth in a press release.
The Amur leopard is “the rarest subspecies of leopard,” according to zoological director Mads Berthelsen.
“Even though the species is experiencing slight growth, there are still only around 110 individuals in the wild,” he said in the press release.
Amur leopards generally live alone in the wild. The newborn cub is still small and blind, however, and is completely dependent on its mother.
The mother spends most of her time with the cub and only leaves for short periods, including to find food.
Because of this, zookeepers are keeping their distance for now. They are monitoring the cub’s development by listening for sounds from the stable.
Zoo visitors will also have to wait before they can see the cub.
“The first weeks are about giving the mother and the cub as much peace as possible. We expect it will take about two months – maybe a little longer – before the cub begins to come out enough that guests can have the opportunity to experience it,” Berthelsen said.
In addition to the approximately 110 Amur leopards known to live in the wild, 93 males and 97 females are kept in zoos around the world, according to the international zoological database Zims.
Only one Amur leopard cub has been registered in the database over the past 12 months, Copenhagen Zoo said.
This does not necessarily mean the animals are having difficulty breeding, Berthelsen said.
“We are increasingly seeing that zoos choose not to let their animals breed because they are concerned about what to do with any surplus offspring,” he said.
The Amur leopard lives mainly in the Primorye region of southeastern Russia. In summer, temperatures in the large forest area can reach 40 degrees Celsius, while winter temperatures can fall below minus 30 degrees.
Cold cuts, filter coffee, chocolate and olive oil were among the products that became cheaper in Denmark in September, according to a monthly analysis by food price monitoring service Madprisluppen.
Overall shelf prices were slightly lower than in August, with the decline most noticeable at discount chains Lidl, 365discount, Rema 1000 and Netto.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com has also lowered prices because it matches the prices of nearly 400 products sold by Rema 1000.
“The cheapest baskets have become cheaper, and the distance from the cheapest to the most expensive basket has grown larger,” Madprisluppen commercial manager Lars Smidt said.
Consumers now pay 27 percent more for the most expensive shopping basket than for the cheapest, with Lidl and Rema 1000 offering the lowest-priced baskets, according to Smidt.
Lidl began cutting prices on a range of products in May as part of its permanent low-price program. Rema 1000, Netto and 365discount soon followed.
A survey conducted by analysis institute Norstat for Lidl found that seven in 10 Danes know about the permanent low-price concept and have bought products at permanent low prices. More than half said they prefer stores with permanent low prices to stores offering frequent special deals.
Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said the chain now has permanent low prices on more than 300 products.
Smidt said it remains uncertain whether grocery prices will continue falling across supermarket chains. Higher oil and gasoline prices could eventually affect food prices, he said.

Denmark could become one of the four largest contributors to the Global Partnership for Education under a new funding plan running through 2030.
The government plans to provide up to 1 billion DKK to the global education fund, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a press release Wednesday.
The funding would begin with 250 million DKK in 2027 and reach a total of up to 1 billion DKK by 2030.
The money is intended to support education in developing countries.
“Education is one of the best investments we can make, both for the children who directly benefit from Denmark’s support, but also for Denmark itself,” Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said during the UN General Assembly in New York.
The funding is included in the government’s proposed 2027 finance bill. It is conditional on the proposal being passed and the funding being approved annually by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The announcement comes as the global education fund faces financial pressure, with several donors expected to reduce their contributions.
Rasmussen said better access to education could also support economic development.
“When more children in the world’s poorest countries go to school and learn to read and do math, it creates fertile ground for economic growth and new markets for Danish business,” he said.
The updated defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. does not introduce new restrictions on how the American military can use its bases in Greenland, according to Danish government officials.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Greenland’s head of government signed the agreement with the U.S. in New York on Tuesday.
The agreement largely confirms rights granted under a 1951 defense deal, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates said.
“But subtracting that, the agreement is an opportunity for the US to establish itself with a military footprint in Greenland, as they already can,” Rasmussen said.
One restriction remains unchanged: nuclear weapons are prohibited in Greenland.
The issue has historical significance. In 1957, Danish Prime Minister H.C. Hansen secretly allowed the U.S. to keep nuclear weapons in Greenland. In 1968, a U.S. B-52 bomber carrying hydrogen bombs crashed near Thule, causing radioactive contamination.
Denmark and the U.S. subsequently agreed that nuclear weapons could not be kept in Greenland.
Rasmussen said the new agreement does not give the U.S. greater military access than it already had.
“The important thing for us is that our nuclear policy is intact, and that in this context we do not give the US any greater access than they actually had beforehand,” he said.
The agreement also introduces stricter requirements for the U.S. to protect Greenland’s environment. American military bases have previously caused pollution affecting local communities.
Before the updated agreement can take effect, it must be approved by Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, and Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.

The security and defense agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark is based on all three parties being members of NATO, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said Tuesday evening.
“If the USA withdraws from the agreement, it thus no longer applies,” Frederiksen said after the agreement was signed.
“It is a very clear premise for this agreement that the countries that have signed the agreement are in NATO. All three countries are now,” she said.
Frederiksen pointed to a change from the original agreement signed in 1951: Greenland is now fully included in the agreement.
“In connection with an independence process, if that situation should arise, this agreement conditions a membership of NATO for an independent Greenland. That is the change,” she said.
“But the entire foundation of the agreement is that we are members of NATO. And I have no expectations that the USA will withdraw from NATO,” Frederiksen said.
The agreement was signed Tuesday by Frederiksen, Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and U.S. President Donald Trump.
The signing took place in New York during the United Nations General Assembly.
After the agreement was signed, Nielsen said that Greenland’s population must now rebuild trust in the United States.

Some 363,600 people who receive prescription allergy medication in Denmark will need to renew their prescriptions if they want to continue receiving a subsidy.
The Danish Medicines Agency announced the changes following a new decision on subsidies for prescription allergy medicines.
Under the new rules, subsidies for some medicines will only be available to specific patient groups, while other patients will no longer be eligible for a subsidy.
If a patient is no longer eligible for a subsidy for their current medicine, they can ask their doctor for a prescription for another medicine with the same effect that is eligible for a subsidy.
Patients who experience side effects or cannot use an alternative for other reasons can have their doctor apply for an individual subsidy.
The changes affect various nasal sprays, eye drops, tablets and capsules, according to the Danish Medicines Agency.
Patients who can use an alternative will no longer be able to receive a subsidy for medicines including Allergone, Altifex, Benadryl, Beconase and Benarhin once the changes take effect on February 1, 2027.
Around 750,000 people in Denmark receive prescription allergy medication. The Danish Medicines Agency encourages patients to check its website to see whether they are affected.
The decision follows a recommendation from the Reimbursement Committee, which advises the Danish Medicines Agency on medicine subsidies.
Deciding which medicines should receive subsidies is part of the Danish Medicines Agency’s routine work.
