articles.title: Ukrainian forces lose about 1,290 troops in special op zone in past day — Defense Ministry
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army lost about 1,290 servicemen over the past day as a result of operations by Russian battlegroups in the special military operation zone, the Defense Ministry said.
According to the report, the enemy lost up to 225 troops in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup North, up to 230 as a result of operations by the Battlegroup West, more than 175 from the Battlegroup South’s actions, over 375 from the Battlegroup Center, more than 240 in the Battlegroup East's area and up to 45 as a result of operations by the Battlegroup Dnepr.
Russian air defenses intercept 244 Ukrainian UAVs over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 244 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot 244 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 244,371 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,019 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,780 multiple rocket launchers, 36,552 field artillery guns and mortars and 72,735 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.
Russian forces hit targets in Kiev, Odessa region overnight
The Russian Armed Forces struck Ukrainian defense industry facilities and logistics centers in Kiev and the Odessa region, as well as vessels, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Last night, as a result of a massive strike with high-precision ground-based and air-based weapons and drones, the Russian Armed Forces hit facilities of Ukraine’s military-industrial complex, telecommunications and logistics centers in Kiev and the Odessa region, as well as vessels operating in the interests of the Ukrainian military," the ministry said in a statement.
Air defenses down 40 Ukrainian drones over Russia overnight
Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 40 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on September 23 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on September 24 (between 5:00 p.m. GMT on September 23 and 5:00 a.m. GMT on September 24), on-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 40 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Tver, Rostov, Krasnodar Regions, as well as Crimea," the statement said.
Russian forces hit tanker delivering fuel, lubricants to Ukrainian military
The Russian Armed Forces struck a tanker at sea that was delivering fuel and lubricants to the Ukrainian military to the Chernomorsk port, the Defense Ministry reported.
"A tanker-type vessel delivering fuel and lubricants intended to supply the Ukrainian military was hit at sea while approaching the port of Chernomorsk," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces hit enterprise in Kiev producing Hornet attack drones
Russian forces struck the Element UA enterprise producing Hornet attack drones, the Defense Ministry reported.
"[Russian forces hit] an industrial enterprise (Element UA LLC) manufacturing and storing components for Hornet medium-range attack unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian Armed Forces struck transport, logistics center in Kiev
The Russian Armed Forces struck a transport and logistics center in Kiev, which was used for storing and distributing UAVs, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The strike in the city of Kiev hit <…> a transport and logistics center used for storing and distributing long- and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russia hits two logistics centers in Odessa storing European military cargo
The Russian Armed Forces struck two logistics centers in Odessa that were storing and distributing European military and dual-use cargo, the Defense Ministry reported.
"[Russian servicemen hit] two logistics centers in the city of Odessa that were storing and distributing military and dual-use cargo arriving in Ukraine from European countries," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian Armed Forces hit Kievstar, Parkovy telecommunications centers
The Russian Armed Forces struck the Kievstar and Parkovy telecommunications centers that provided communication services and processing capacity to the Ukrainian army, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The strike in the city of Kiev hit <…> the Kievstar and Parkovy telecommunications centers that provided communication services and processing capacity to the Ukrainian army," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces hit Kiev facility that manufactures drone components
The Russian Armed Forces struck production and storage facilities for long-range drones in Kiev, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The following targets were hit as a result of the strike: an industrial facility in Kiev that manufactures components for long-range and medium-range drones and prepares ground-based robotic systems for deployment, a drone production facility (Pegasus Arms LLC) that manufactures and stores long-range and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles, including fixed-wing models," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian Armed Forces take control of Buzovo, Khizhnyakovo in Kharkov Region
The Battlegroup North has secured control over Buzovo and Khizhnyakovo, located within an encircled area in the Kharkov Region.
"As a result of active operations, the communities of Buzovo and Khizhnyakovo in the Kharkov Region - located within an encircled area - have been brought under control," the Defense Ministry said.
Russian forces liberate Zaporozhye Region’s Svetlaya Dolina
Russia’s battlegroup East liberated the settlement of Svetlaya Dolina in the Zaporozhye Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The battlegroup East continued to advance deep into enemy defenses and liberated Svetlaya Dolina in the Zaporozhye Region," the statement said.
Russian forces repel Kiev troops’ attempts to break out of encirclement near Svyatogorovka
Russia’s Battlegroup Center has repelled attempts by the Ukrainian National Guard to break out towards Svyatogorovka in the Donetsk People's Republic (DPR), the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"Further attempts by units of the enemy's 4th and 15th National Guard brigades to break out of the encirclement towards Svyatogorovka in the Donetsk People's Republic have been repelled," the statement reads.
Russian forces fighting for Rublenoye, Khripuny settlements in Kharkov Region
Russia’s Battlegroup North continues fighting to liberate the communities of Rublenoye and Khripuny in the Kharkov Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Combat operations are underway to liberate the settlements of Rublenoye and Khripuny in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces approach Reznikovo, where large enemy forces are concentrated
While tightening the encirclement in the Kharkov Region, Russia’s battlegroup North approached Reznikovo, a village where large Ukrainian military forces are concentrated, the Defense Ministry reported.
"While tightening the encirclement, the battlegroup North has has come very close to the village of Reznikovo, where large Ukrainian military forces are concentrated," the statement said.
Russian forces clear 152 buildings near Dobropolye in DPR over past day
Russian forces cleared 152 buildings near the settlement of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR) over the past day, the Defense Ministry said.
"Near the settlement of Dobropolye, units of the 51st Army expanded the external encirclement ring as a result of offensive operations. <...> More than 45 Ukrainian troops were eliminated and 152 buildings were cleared over the past day," the ministry said.
Russian forces keep fighting to liberate three settlements in Kharkov Region
Units of the Russian Battlegroup North continue combat operations to expand the external control zone and liberate the Petropavlovka, Prikolotnoye and Lozovaya communities in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Combat operations to expand the external control zone and liberate the Petropavlovka, Prikolotnoye and Lozovaya communities in the Kharkov Region are ongoing," according to the ministry’s statement.
Ukraine loses German-made Leopard tank in special military operation zone
Russia’s Battlegroup South destroyed a German-made Leopard tank in its area of responsibility over the past day in the special military operation in Ukraine, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Overall, the enemy lost more than 175 personnel, two tanks, including a German-made Leopard tank, two Kozak armored combat vehicles and 23 motor vehicles," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces liberate Dobropolye settlement in DPR
Russia’s battlegroup Center has expanded the encirclement and liberated the Dobropolye settlement in the Donetsk People’s Republic’ near the city of the same name, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Near the city of Dobropolye, the 51st Army expanded the encirclement and liberated the Dobropolye settlement in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the statement said.
Russian Armed Forces hit storage sites for Ukrainian army’s long-, medium-range UAVs
The Russian forces struck storage sites for the Ukrainian army’s long-and medium-range unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and their components, as well as temporary deployment points for Ukrainian armed groups and foreign mercenaries in 140 areas, in the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Operational-tactical aviation, combat unmanned aerial vehicles, the missile troops and artillery of the Russian Armed Forces’ battlegroups struck ammunition and fuel depots, energy facilities supporting the Ukrainian army, storage sites for long-and medium-range UAVs and their components, as well as temporary deployment points for Ukrainian armed groups and foreign mercenaries in 140 areas," the report said.

articles.title: EU countries agree to release long-stalled €6.6 billion in military aid for Ukraine
articles.body:
The decision to release €6.6 billion through the European Peace Facility comes at a critical juncture for Ukraine, which is grappling with a significant shortfall in its Ministry of Defence budget that could jeopardize drone deliveries.
European Union countries have agreed to release a €6.6 billion programme of military aid for Ukraine that had stalled since spring 2023, when Hungary imposed a controversial veto that paralysed the initiative.
The agreement at the political level was reached on Friday during a meeting of the Political and Security Committee in Brussels.
"That's good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia," High Representative Kaja Kallas wrote on social media, announcing the news.
"Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite."
The so-called European Peace Facility (EPF) was designed to partially reimburse weapons and ammunition that member states donate to Ukraine.
In the early years of the war, the EPF was considered one of the bloc's central lines of assistance and was regularly topped up with fresh money.
But in May 2023, Hungary, under then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, slapped a veto that stopped the scheme dead in its tracks.
Budapest complained about Kyiv's decision to add OTP Bank, Hungary's largest commercial bank, to its list of "international sponsors of war". The name-shaming catalogue was discontinued in 2024 after pushback from Western allies.
Still, Hungary kept its veto in place, angering other capitals. The EPF eventually fell off the radar as Brussels set up new assistance programmes.
The deadlock was broken only this year when Orbán lost the parliamentary elections in April, and Prime Minister Péter Magyar came to power. Since then, member states have been negotiating the terms for the release of the €6.6 billion.
According to Kallas, the agreement reached on Friday splits the pot into three strands:
- €4.7 billion for reimbursements
- €1 billion for joint procurement of military equipment
- €900 million for the EU mission that trains Ukraine's armed forces
Some countries will wire their share of €4.7 billion in reimbursements directly to Ukraine, Kallas said without naming them.
Several legislative acts need to be adopted before the money is actually released.
The news comes at a precarious time for Ukraine, which is staring down a $27 billion (€23.67 billion) shortfall in its Ministry of Defence.
The European Commission and the International Monetary Fund are in talks with the Ukrainian government to determine a possible solution.
On Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned the budget crunch needed to be resolved between October and November to pay for drone deliveries scheduled for the first three months of 2027.
"Everyone understands that Ukraine cannot be left on its own and that more must be invested in Ukrainian-made drones and missiles, because most of this deficit is precisely the funding needed for weapons," Zelenskyy said.
"Everyone understands how difficult it is to get through this period amid constant strikes. Ukraine will not be left alone."

articles.title: Zelensky says Trump made ‘final decision’ to give Ukraine Patriot licence
articles.body:
Zelensky says Trump made ‘final decision’ to give Ukraine Patriot licence
- Ukrainian President Zelensky confirmed that US President Trump made the "final decision" to grant Ukraine licences to produce advanced Patriot missiles amid urgent defence needs.
- Kyiv faces a severe shortage of Patriot missiles to counter Russia’s growing drone and missile attacks, with immediate needs unmet despite potential future production.
- A recent Russian drone strike killed a 14-year-old in Kyiv, prompting Zelensky to condemn it as a "savage and sickening strike," highlighting the ongoing civilian suffering and technological warfare.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sept 25 said US President Donald Trump told him he would allow Ukraine to produce advanced Patriot air defence missiles, after a series of reversals on the issue.
Kyiv is facing a shortage of the missiles, needed to counter Russia’s increasing drone and missile attacks on the country, the latest of which killed a 14-year-old boy in the capital on Sept 25.
Zelensky during his latest visit to the United States this week renewed calls for air defence support, and for the Patriots, which remain the only system reliably able to counter Russia’s powerful ballistic missiles.
“At our last meeting, President Trump emphasised to me that yes, I have made a final decision. Ukraine will receive licences for the production of Patriot missiles,” Zelensky said in a voice note to journalists.
In July, Trump said it would be “pretty cool” to grant Ukraine the licences, before backtracking, saying the US should be “very careful” before granting Ukraine authorisation.
Ukraine has reported an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in February, diverting supplies of the advanced systems.
Even if the licences are granted, establishing industrial capacity would require more than a year and would not meet Kyiv’s immediate needs.
And Kyiv, preparing for winter, has renewed calls for urgent support.
It needs 5 per cent of the US’ Patriot interceptor missiles to get through the winter and 10 per cent to destroy all of Russia’s ballistic projectiles, Zelensky said in August.
‘Savage and sickening strike’
Moscow has also been aiming at the capital with newly developed jet-powered drones, which have succeeded in bypassing some of the drone interception systems developed by Ukraine.
While it used to target Kyiv mainly during the hours of darkness, Moscow now often attacks in broad daylight.
As people were making their way to work on the morning of Sept 25, a drone struck a residential building in the city, killing a 14-year-old boy.
Zelensky denounced the attack, calling it “an absolutely savage and sickening strike, devoid of any military logic”.
AFP journalists on the spot saw residents gathering around a multi-storey building, with apartments on the ninth and 10th floors left charred by the attack.
Mykyta Sysoyev was smoking a cigarette outside his damaged building.
The 23-year-old IT specialist said he was woken up by an explosion but only realised the strike had hit his own building when he checked the news.
“My jaw dropped a bit,” he said. “It’s strange: on the one hand, I’ve got used to it, but on the other, people are constantly dying.”
Asked about the increase in drone strikes, he added: “This is a technological race and a technological war... Unfortunately, people will suffer while we’re searching for solutions.”
In the southern region of Odesa, another person was killed in a repeated strike on a postal facility, the authorities said. AFP

articles.title: Zelenskyy broke confidentiality with N. Korea POWs disclosure: S. Korea
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy broke a confidentiality agreement by disclosing publicly that Kyiv had sent North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, the East Asian country's president said Thursday.
The remarks by President Lee Jae Myung came after Zelenskyy told the United Nations that two North Korean soldiers had been recently sent to South Korea after being captured while fighting for Russia in the war against Ukraine.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die," Zelenskyy said in his speech.
Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be captured alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelenskyy said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to send them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishment the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
The revelation prompted South Korea's political opposition to criticize the Lee administration for allowing a foreign leader to inform them of the prisoners' arrivals.
South Korean president said it was "deeply regretful" that Ukraine had made the transfer public, adding that the two sides had agreed not to disclose it.
"I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," Lee said on the social media platform X.
"The issue of bringing North Korean prisoners to South Korea is a highly sensitive one that could have a major impact on diplomacy, security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula," he said.
Lee said there had been calls to disclose the arrivals, but "given the problems that could arise from making it public, we agreed that keeping it confidential was the right thing to do."
Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn told journalists that Ukraine was "an open country" and that it would have been strange to hand over the soldiers in secret.
"From the entire story – which is long and detailed – we reported only the fact itself, that they were sent to the Republic of Korea," he said.
A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South.
Under South Korea's constitution, all Koreans, including those living in the North, are considered citizens, and officials have said this would apply to any North Korean troops captured in Ukraine.
The transfer comes as South Korea has voiced support for efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea and U.S. President Donald Trump has renewed his willingness to engage with Pyongyang.
Opposition politicians in South Korea questioned why Seoul had not announced the matter first.
South Korean opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told reporters on Thursday that the two men had left Ukraine last weekend, transited through a third country and arrived in South Korea three to four days ago, Yonhap News Agency reported.
"While their exact location is unknown, I believe our intelligence agencies are protecting them," Yu was quoted as saying.
South Korea said in June it would accept any North Korean prisoners of war captured after fighting for Russia and opposed their repatriation to either Russia or North Korea.
In his address, Zelenskyy criticized North Korea's deployment of troops to support Moscow.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000-15,000 troops to support Russia's war since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Pyongyang has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, as well as ballistic missiles, long-range artillery systems and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.

articles.title: Latvia moves to buy Anduril’s Barracuda cruise missiles
articles.body:
- Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said Latvia expects to complete the purchase of Anduril's Barracuda long-range cruise missiles after visiting the company.
- He also witnessed the signing of cooperation memoranda involving Latvia's Ministry of Defense and Latvian drone maker Origin Robotics.
Latvia is working to buy Anduril’s Barracuda long-range cruise missiles, President Edgars Rinkēvičs said after visiting the American defense company and meeting its founder, Palmer Luckey.
Rinkēvičs wrote that he looked forward to completing the acquisition of the missiles and to further defense industry cooperation. During the visit he also witnessed the signing of memoranda of cooperation involving Latvia’s Ministry of Defense and Origin Robotics, a Latvian drone maker. Neither Latvia nor Anduril has disclosed which Barracuda version Latvia wants, how many missiles it plans to buy, the price or a delivery date. The terms of the memoranda were not made public.
Barracuda is a family of turbojet-powered, subsonic cruise missiles that Anduril unveiled in September 2024 in three sizes: Barracuda-100, -250 and -500. The largest carries a warhead of more than 45 kg (99 pounds) over 926 km (575 miles). Anduril designed the missiles to be built quickly and in large numbers, and says the three versions share more than 90% of their components. The company claims Barracuda costs about 30% less and takes half the time to produce compared with similar cruise missiles.
The missiles can be launched from fighter jets, helicopters, cargo aircraft, ships and ground launchers. Anduril says they can fly together and split roles on a single mission, with some acting as decoys or scouts while others strike.
Barracuda is moving into large-scale production. In May, the U.S. Department of War signed a framework agreement for Anduril to deliver at least 1,000 surface-launched Barracuda-500Ms a year for three years to the U.S. Army, starting in 2027. In July, Poland’s state-owned defense group PGZ signed an agreement to assemble and later produce the Barracuda-500M at its Military Aviation Works No. 2 plant in Bydgoszcz. PGZ said European production could make the missile eligible for purchase by other EU countries under the bloc’s SAFE defense loan program.
Origin Robotics, based in Riga, builds drones for military use. Its BEAK drone is already in combat service in Ukraine. The company has also developed BLAZE, a briefcase-sized drone interceptor that uses radar and AI-based cameras to find and hit enemy drones on its own after launch.
Latvia borders Russia and Belarus. Its longest-range strike weapon on order is the Army Tactical Missile System, a ballistic missile with a range of about 300 km (186 miles) that Latvia is buying along with six HIMARS launchers under a deal approved by the U.S. State Department in 2023. The Barracuda-500 would give Latvian forces roughly three times that reach.

articles.title: Iranian flights cancelled as new US 'D-Day' sanctions take effect, Saudis say they shoot down Houthi missiles
articles.body:
New US sanctions shut down Iranian flights
DUBAI/RIYADH, Sept 24 - Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the UAE and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of a shift in US policy to target companies in third countries that do business with Iran.
The General Civil Aviation Authority of the United Arab Emirates, the Middle East's biggest travel hub, said that as a result of the new US policy it was suspending all flights by Iranian airlines until further notice.
Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that flights had also been shut down to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan, and to the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It said authorities were working to route flights to another Iraqi airport, in Najaf, a major Shi'ite Muslim religious pilgrimage site.
Washington had announced it would put sanctions on any global companies doing business with Iranian airlines after September 23, with the aim of grounding Iran's entire civil fleet worldwide.
Other countries in the Gulf region also appeared to have restricted flights.
Tehran's Imam Khomeini Airport listed scheduled arrivals and departures on Thursday to and from countries including Afghanistan, Armenia, China, Iraq, Pakistan, Tajikistan and Turkey. But no flights appeared to be listed to or from the nearby Gulf states, with which Iran has long had some of its most important business and travel ties.
Iran has suggested that enforcement of a US-mandated air blockade would lead to potential escalation. On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official threatened to make airports "unusable" in any regional country that abides by the US ban.
Separately on Thursday, authorities in Saudi Arabia said they had intercepted intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthi fighters. The Houthis said they had fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets. An escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has emerged this month as the combat zone in the wider Middle East war.
'ECONOMIC D-DAY'
With the US-Israeli war against Iran largely stalemated for months on the battlefield, Washington has announced a shift in tactics to extend the reach of its financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms, a practice known as "secondary sanctions".
Trump referred to the new strategy last month as "economic D-Day", comparing it to the assault on Nazi-controlled France in World War Two by the United States and its allies.
A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran's isolation and worsen an economic crisis in the country, which is already facing a US blockade of its ports at sea.
"We are living in an open-air prison," a retired teacher in Tehran told Reuters by text message on condition her name not be used.
SAUDI ARABIA SAYS IT SHOOTS DOWN HOUTHI MISSILES
The war, which Trump launched alongside Israel in February as "Operation Epic Fury", has disrupted global energy supplies, killed thousands of people and pushed up oil prices.
Conflicts have been reignited in other regional countries where Iran has allies, initially in Lebanon and now in Yemen, where the Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia in July and launched a lightning advance this month against a Saudi-backed government.
The Houthis have repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia this month, and say the Saudi air force has conducted hundreds of strikes on Yemen since fighting escalated.
Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles on Thursday, after issuing emergency alerts for areas including the holy city of Mecca, Jeddah and Yanbu, the main Saudi Red Sea oil port.
"Any escalation and violations by the terrorist Houthi militia will be dealt with firmly," a Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen said in a statement.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had attacked Saudi military sites in Jazan province bordering Yemen, targeting operations rooms, command and control centres, weapons depots, missile launch sites and military camps.
Sources in the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed Yemeni government said their forces had repelled overnight Houthi attacks on a key supply route to Aden, the Indian Ocean port city where the government is based.
The Houthis, who already controlled the north including the capital Sanaa, seized Yemen's entire Red Sea coast this month and have been pushing into adjacent highlands near the central mountain city of Taiz and the road from Aden.
The Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces holding a steep winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for hemmed in pro-government forces, and for goods entering Taiz.
Seizing parts of the Taiz-Aden road could allow the Houthis to tighten their grip around Taiz and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast.
More than 700 people have been killed and thousands wounded in the latest fighting, according to the United Nations. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have been displaced within the country, while more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa. REUTERS

articles.title: France to send military to protect Saudi Arabia, Macron says
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
France to send military to protect Saudi Arabia on Red Sea oil route, Macron says
France will send troops and defence systems to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which is key for energy transport, French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday.
Macron also said a US ban on diesel exports, which the White House has denied is under consideration, would be "catastrophic," both globally and for the US economy.
Macron was speaking in a wide-ranging primetime television interview on the international situation, in which he also warned about possible Russian attacks on French soil.
Facing growing pressure at home over high energy prices, Macron sought to assure the French that France had adequate gas and oil supplies as winter approaches. He said Paris was actively working to ensure flows were not disrupted.
Crude oil prices have surged recently as the main alternative route for Saudi oil exports through Yanbu has come under missile attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
"We are going to send military resources, that is to say, soldiers, radar systems and defence systems, to protect this site - not to get us involved in any conflicts, but to protect this site," Macron told TF1 and France 2 TV.
RUSSIAN THREAT
Macron dismissed a report by Spanish newspaper El Mundo that the US Central Intelligence Agency had warned European governments about the threat of potential drone attacks from the Mediterranean.
"I can deny it. The CIA did not inform French services," he said.
Still, Macron said Russia is multiplying hostile and criminal acts against European countries, and France could face strikes similar to the failed attack in Leipzig. Germany said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack in August on the Leipzig airport.
Macron gathered French party chiefs at the Elysee last week to brief them on the growing threat from Russia. He later said he had ordered his government to draw up a plan to protect critical infrastructure against drone and cyber attacks.
Macron said Moscow was seeking to intimidate Europe and break the continent's resolve in supporting Ukraine.
Russia says European allegations of hybrid attacks are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
Yet Macron's position on Russia was weakened this week after France shocked other EU members by getting Russian-Uzbek metals tycoon Alisher Usmanov exempted from EU sanctions, citing national security concerns. That prompted Azerbaijan to pardon a French national jailed for espionage.

articles.title: Chinese copy of Russia’s Tor air defense system seen in Algerian colors
articles.body:
- Photos on Chinese social media show an HQ-17 air defense system in camouflage matching Algerian equipment, with Chinese sources saying it is for Algeria.
- Neither Algeria nor China's CASIC has confirmed a sale, and the quantity and delivery date remain unknown.
A Chinese HQ-17 short-range air defense system painted in camouflage matching Algerian military vehicles has appeared in photos shared widely on Weibo, with Chinese sources claiming the system is headed to Algeria.
The photos were highlighted by an OSINT defense account, which noted that the camouflage pattern matches the paint used on a large number of Chinese-made weapons already in Algerian service. The other sources acknowledged a small possibility that the vehicles belong to an export order for a country in Africa’s Sahel region that uses similar camouflage. It also said reports that Algeria operates the HQ-17 had circulated before.
The HQ-17 is a Chinese development of the Russian Tor-M1, a mobile system that detects, tracks and fires on low-flying threats from a single vehicle. China bought 27 Tor-M1 systems from Russia in two contracts in 1996 and 1999, then developed its own version. CASIC built it to shoot down aircraft, helicopters and drones as well as cruise missiles, guided bombs and air-to-surface missiles.
Each launch vehicle carries its own radar and eight missiles, so it can fight without support from other units, though it can also take targeting data from separate surveillance radars. The Chinese version uses an electronically scanned radar designed to resist jamming. The missile reaches Mach 3 and can engage targets between 1.5 km and 20 km (1 to 12 miles) away, at altitudes up to 10 km (33,000 feet).
The People’s Liberation Army Ground Force operates the tracked HQ-17 and the wheeled HQ-17A, which rides on a 6×6 truck and can fire while moving. China first showed an export version, the FM-2000, at the 2018 Zhuhai Airshow and cleared a variant called the HQ-17AE for export in 2021. The HQ-17AE can guide four missiles against four targets at the same time. Serbia operates the HQ-17AE, and the system has also been reported in Saudi Arabia and Tajikistan.
Algeria runs one of the largest air defense networks in Africa, built on both Russian and Chinese equipment. Its long-range layer reportedly includes Russian S-300PMU-2 and S-400 systems alongside the Chinese HQ-9, with Russian Buk-M2 systems at medium range. Algeria has also fielded Chinese CHL-906 electronic warfare vehicles, which its Ministry of National Defense showed during an exercise in the country’s southwest.
A short-range system such as the HQ-17 would sit at the bottom of that network, protecting units and key sites from drones, helicopters and incoming missiles that get past the longer-range layers.

articles.title: US arms sales to Israel surge to $21.6 bn in 20 months
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US arms sales to Israel worth $21.6 billion in 20 months
Notifications submitted by the US President Donald Trump administration to Congress, along with US State Department data covering the period from 20 January 2025 to 17 September 2026, show that the Trump administration has approved arms deals for Israel worth $21.6 billion in just 20 months.
The value of military aid, funded by US taxpayers, and arms deals approved by former President Joe Biden for Israel between October 2023 and early 2025 exceeded $17.9 billion, according to a study by Brown University.
These weapons were used in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of more than 50,000 civilians, children and women during this period.
September 2026: $2.8 billion in weapons
The US State Department informally notified the offices of the four top Republican and Democratic members in the House of Representatives and Senate last week of a $2.8 billion military aid deal involving new weapons for Israel that Washington is preparing to conclude.
The deal includes 40,000 2,000-pound bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrating warheads.
A 2,000-pound bomb is considered one of the most destructive munitions in the world, as its explosion sends metal fragments thousands of feet in all directions and can penetrate metal and thick concrete.
Despite opposition from Democrats, the deal is expected to pass as usual under emergency authority that allows the administration to bypass congressional objections.
Historically, Congress has failed to stop any arms deal.
The following are the main previous large deals:
January 2025: $2.04 billion
After the Biden administration had previously sent shipments of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, and as criticism mounted following their use in the genocide in Gaza and the killing of tens of thousands of children and women, his administration suspended one shipment in 2024.
In the first week of the Trump administration after his return to the White House in January 2025, he announced the immediate lifting of the ban on that shipment.
The shipment was valued at $2.04 billion.
February 2025: $7.4 billion
In the first week of February 2025, the US State Department informed Congress in two separate statements that it had approved an arms deal for Israel worth $7.4 billion.
It included 20,000 bombs, guidance systems and equipment worth $6.75 billion, and 3,000 Hellfire air-to-ground missiles worth $660 million.
The administration bypassed congressional notification to obtain approval.
The Trump administration used emergency powers that allow for immediate sales, citing national security interests, to bypass the usual congressional review procedures.
It provided Israel with a $675 million deal including 5,000 1,000-pound bombs and guidance kits and a $295 million deal including Caterpillar bulldozers.
The deal was announced at a value of $3.01 billion, but it included what the administration had announced in January 2025.
June 2025: $510 million
Following the US-Israeli attack on Iran in June 2025, and to rebuild Israel's stockpile, the Trump administration approved the provision of high-precision guidance systems to the Israeli military, worth $510 million.
The deal included more than 7,000 guidance kits for offensive munitions.
January 2026: $6.67 billion
In September 2025, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources, that the Trump administration was seeking congressional approval for an arms deal with Israel worth more than $6 billion.
The deal would be funded through the Foreign Military Financing programme, or military aid.
In January, the deal was announced with a total value of $6.67 billion. It includes 30 Apache helicopters, doubling Israel's fleet of this type of aircraft, 3,250 assault vehicles and other equipment.
March 2026: $650 million
One week after the US-Israeli war on Iran began this year, Israel requested more than 20,000 bombs.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, as stated in a statement in March 2026, determined that an emergency existed requiring the sale to Israel to be completed immediately and the deal to be exempted from congressional review.
The deal was announced at a value of $650 million and included 12,000 1,000-pound bombs, as well as 500-pound bombs.
Reuters also quoted an official as saying that Israel would purchase an additional $298 million worth of munitions through direct sales.
May 2026: $992 million
On 1 May, Rubio again used emergency powers to approve a deal for Israel to purchase 10,000 APKWS laser-guided rocket systems worth $992.4 million.
These rockets have been used as countermeasures against Iranian drones because of their lower cost compared with expensive weapons.
This means that the total value of the deals announced and approved by the administration so far is $19.2 billion.
It will rise to $21.6 billion when the administration completes procedures for the latest deal, with at least half of the amount being military aid funded by US taxpayers.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
articles.body:
Finnish leader pleads with Musk to help Ukraine hit Russian missile launchers
NEW YORK, Sept 24 - Finnish President Alexander Stubb said on Thursday he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside Russian territory.
With winter looming, Ukraine has an acute shortage of air defenses to repel Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv officials believe that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the Russian launchers that fire the missiles.
"That's why ... I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers, either in the occupied territory of Ukraine or in Russia for strategic purposes because that would save lives," Stubb said.
The Finnish leader, a staunch ally of Ukraine who also has good relations with US President Donald Trump, made the remark in an interview with Reuters in New York where world leaders have converged for the annual gathering at the United Nations.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy used the event to press hard for ceasefires that would cover strikes on targets related to energy infrastructure and vessels in the Black Sea. Russia has given no public indication it wants to see such arrangements.
Four-and-a-half years since the full-scale Russian invasion, the Ukrainians fear Moscow plans to systematically target and destroy power and heating sites in the depth of winter. Russia's use of ballistic missiles hit record levels this summer.
Only Ukraine's Patriot air defenses are able to intercept such missiles, but ammunition is severely depleted and it is unclear where new supplies could come from.
Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over Ukraine shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine's battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones.
Starlink does not work over Russian territory, but Ukrainian officials believe turning it on for Ukraine's use inside Russia would allow its weapons to strike mobile ballistic launchers located within several hundred kilometres of the border.
Looking ahead to winter, Stubb said there were three things that Ukraine needed.
"One is air defenses and even Starlink would be to a certain extent a good air defense there. And the second one is energy installations for the winter."
"The third one is money. So those are the things that we're working on. We're working on putting up a winter package because I don't see the war ending, you know, before the winter."
Stubb said it was good that US-led peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine had restarted in August with the visits of US envoys to both Moscow and Kyiv.
"I still think that the easiest solution would be to call an unconditional ceasefire, basically stop the killing, as President Trump reiterated in his speech in the UN General Assembly," he said.
Such a step, he continued, would be followed by negotiations on security, territory, reconstruction and compensation and other topics.
The war could be frozen along the line of contact with 30-kilometre buffer zones east and west, he said, adding that the next best option was the idea of the partial ceasefire on energy and grain related targets. REUTERS

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim to have launched missiles, drones at Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Thursday that the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said were aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea.
The Houthis later on Thursday said they had carried out attacks on what they described as "a sensitive target" in the capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group used ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones in the two operations, adding that they had achieved their objectives.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on Riyadh. Saudi civil defense did not issue an emergency alert for Riyadh on Thursday.
The escalation threatens Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil through the Red Sea at a time when the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, and the kingdom's East-West pipeline is only now resuming operations after drone strikes earlier this month. The Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, opening a second theater in the US-Iran war.
It was not clear whether there was any damage or casualties in either Taif or Yanbu, the main alternative route for Saudi oil, after a widespread emergency alert was issued for areas including Jeddah and the holy city of Mecca.
The attack on Yanbu followed an improvement in prospects for oil exports to resume from the terminal there. Industry sources say Saudi Arabia is building up crude pumping volumes through its East-West pipeline, which was shut on September 11 after drone attacks which Riyadh has blamed on Iraqi militia.
Houthi terrorists claim attack on Jazan further south
Saree had said earlier on Thursday that the group had attacked Saudi military sites in Jazan province bordering Yemen. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saree said the Houthis carried out the attack using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones, targeting what he described as "operations rooms, command and control centers, weapons depots" in Jazan, as well as missile launch sites and military camps.
Saudi civil defense issued an emergency alert over a potential danger in Jazan on Wednesday, but it issued no alerts on Thursday.
Civil defense authorities also warned of potential danger in the northwestern province of Tabuk, near the border with Jordan – a first for the area during the latest escalation between the kingdom and the Houthis this month.
The Houthis have largely attacked southern areas of Saudi Arabia.
They seized the whole Yemeni western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab el-Mandeb waterway.
Flare-up in Yemen's civil war broadens Middle East conflict
The Riyadh-backed government's forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen's third-biggest city, Taiz, from the southern port city of Aden, where the internationally recognized administration is based, government sources said.
The Houthis have kept up pressure along a steep, winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for government forces and the only route for goods and residents to reach Taiz and travel abroad.
Seizing parts of the road could allow the Houthis to tighten their grip around the city and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast.
The fighting is the latest episode in 12 years of civil war in Yemen, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce. The Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year in support of the internationally recognized government.
More than 700 people have been killed and thousands wounded in the latest fighting, according to the United Nations. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have been displaced within the country, while more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says intercepted 6 Houthi ballistic missiles targeting Taif, Yanbu
articles.body:

articles.title: Finland, Sweden Intercept Russian Military Aircraft Together for First Time
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Finland, Sweden Intercept Russian Military Aircraft Together for First Time
Finnish and Swedish Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) fighter jets carried out their first joint operational identification mission on September 24, intercepting a formation of Russian military aircraft in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Finnish Air Force's Air Operations Center led the mission, pairing Finnish F/A-18 Hornet fighters with Swedish JAS 39 Gripen jets, according to a release from the Swedish Armed Forces published on September 25.
Colonel Vesa Mäntylä, Deputy Chief of Staff at Air Force Command Finland, explained that the two air forces are responsible for surveillance and protection of their nations' airspace.
"The deeper cooperation that began this autumn enables joint identification missions," Mäntylä stated, noting the arrangement also lets QRA jets operate from the other country's air bases.
Major General Jonas Wikman, Commander of the Swedish Air Force, called the mission a testament to years of trust between the two forces.
"We can now operate seamlessly together – as air forces, as nations and as Allies," Wikman added.
According to the release, the QRA jets identified a Russian detachment operating over the Gulf of Finland. The formation included:
- a Tu-134 transport aircraft, NATO reporting name "Crusty";
- MiG-31 fighter jets, reporting name "Foxhound";
- Su-30 fighter jets, reporting name "Flanker-H."
The MiG-31 is a twin-engine, long-range interceptor built to defend Russian airspace and escort strategic bombers. It can exceed Mach 2.8 and typically carries long-range R-37 air-to-air missiles. Its presence over the Gulf points to continued Russian use of the corridor for high-speed patrol and escort work near NATO's northern border.
The Su-30 is a twin-seat, multirole fighter suited to both air superiority and strike missions, with a mixed weapons load and an extended combat radius. Its inclusion suggests the detachment combined an armed fighter escort with the transport flight rather than a single-purpose sortie.
Finland's F/A-18 Hornets and Sweden's JAS 39 Gripens serve as each country's primary QRA interceptors, both built for rapid scramble and beyond-visual-range engagement.
Flying them jointly, with cross-basing rights now in place, shortens response times across the shared Baltic approach, the release noted.
The identification mission fits into a broader Nordic Air Power framework linking Finland, Sweden, Norway and Denmark to NATO's collective defense structure.
Finnish and Swedish crews have flown near-weekly Cross Border Training sorties for several years, and both air forces coordinate with NATO's Baltic Air Policing detachments across the region, according to the release.
In late August, Sweden's government ordered military units, including JAS 39 Gripen fighters and naval vessels, to patrol areas along Finland's border with Russia.
The deployment followed a direct request from Finnish authorities amid repeated Russian airspace violations tied to the war, and rested on bilateral agreements giving Swedish forces a mandate to help defend Finnish territory.

articles.title: Zelensky: Most of Ukraine's budget deficit is funding for weapons
articles.body:
Zelensky: Most of Ukraine's budget deficit is funding for weapons
The head of state said this while speaking to the media, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"I had several meetings – with business representatives, financial groups, IMF Managing Director Kristalina [Georgieva], and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. There has been a positive and constructive response from the EU and the International Monetary Fund. Everyone understands that it is very important to cover this deficit. Everyone understands that Ukraine cannot be left on its own, that we need to invest more in Ukrainian-made drones and missiles. Because most of this deficit is precisely funding for weapons. Everyone understands how difficult this period is and how difficult it is to withstand the constant strikes," he said.
Zelensky stressed that Ukraine would not go through this period alone. In particular, he said, EU support would continue, while the IMF would continue its programs.
The president said that going forward, the prime minister, together with the finance minister and the head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, would work out all the details concerning coverage of the deficit. According to him, some of these funds could be raised through the Drone Deal framework. The head of state added that the Ukrainian team was working on the details and that a meeting with the European team was planned in Ukraine or Belgium in the near future.
As reported, the budget deficit of Ukraine's Ministry of Defense currently stands at $27 billion.

articles.title: Stubb asks Musk to allow to use Starlink to launch strikes deep into Russia
articles.body:
LONDON, September 25. /TASS/. Finnish President Alexander Stubb has appealed to US entrepreneur Elon Musk to expand the coverage area of the Starlink satellite internet service to help Kiev launch strikes deep into Russia, Reuters reported.
"I plead that Elon Musk would give the Ukrainians the possibility to use Starlink in areas where there are ballistic missile launchers," the news agency quoted Stubb as saying.
The Finnish leader also noted that Ukraine needs air defense capabilities, and extending Starlink coverage across the entire territory of Russia could help repel attacks by the Russian Armed Forces. In addition, Stubb stated that Kiev is in dire need of power generation facilities for the winter and financial assistance.
In recent months, Vladimir Zelensky has repeatedly asked US President Donald Trump for permission to use Starlink capabilities to launch strikes deep into Russian territory.
