articles.title: Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
On 30 March, Kosovo’s government approved the deployment of Kosovo Security Forces personnel to Gaza as part of the proposed International Stabilisation Force (ISF) backed by the United States and envisioned under President Donald J. Trump’s peace plan.
Then on 7 September, Pristina formally signed an agreement to join the United Nations-mandated force, according to a statement posted on social media by the Board of Peace.
The decision places Kosovo at the centre of a wider international effort to establish security and support reconstruction in Gaza, while also raising questions about the mission’s role, its legal and political implications, and Kosovo’s ties with the United States and Israel.
Kosovo's strategic calculation
Kosovo’s decision to join the Board of Peace and the ISF underscores Pristina’s commitment to the United States. The small Muslim-majority Balkan state has long regarded Washington as its most important international partner.
This is particularly because of the US role in supporting Kosovo during and after the Kosovo War (1998–99) and in backing its independence, which the US under the George W. Bush administration formally recognised in February 2008 as one of the first countries in the world to do so.
But Dr Ramadan Ilazi, head of research at the Kosovar Centre for Security Studies (KCSS), said Kosovo’s decision should not be understood solely as an attempt to please Washington.
He described the motivation as a combination of principle, pragmatism, and strategic interest, arguing that Kosovo also wants to demonstrate that it can contribute to international security after more than two decades as a recipient of international assistance.
“There is now a strong desire to demonstrate that it can also be a contributor. Kosovo remains grateful for the international engagement that helped end the war in 1999, supported post-war reconstruction, and continues to provide security through KFOR. Participating in the ISF is therefore also a way of expressing solidarity and giving something back,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Lily Lynch, editor-in-chief of the Balkanist Magazine, holds that participating in Trump’s initiative sends a message that Kosovo’s relationship with the United States is intended to remain strong regardless of which political party controls the White House.
This is quite significant given concerns in Kosovo that a Trump administration could potentially be more accommodating toward Serbia.
“Kosovo decided to join the Board of Peace and [ISF] as a demonstration of its fidelity to the United States. The decision indicates that regardless of who is in the White House, Kosovo's commitment to its relationship with the United States is ironclad,” she told The New Arab.
“Some foreign policy commentators see Kosovo's existence as an independent state as a product of Clintonite foreign policy and liberal internationalism; there was concern among some in Kosovo that a Trump presidency would give Serbia an advantage,” added Lynch.
“But participation in the Board of Peace and ISF suggests that Kosovo wants to make clear that its commitment to a strong relationship with America transcends party politics.”
The Kosovo-Gaza comparison and its limits
Prime Minister Albin Kurti has framed the decision through Kosovo’s own experience with international peacekeeping. In announcing the government’s support for the deployment, Kurti pointed to the fact that Kosovo itself has benefited from international forces since 1999.
The analogy is also linked to the continued presence of NATO’s KFOR mission, which has provided security in Kosovo for more than two-and-a-half decades.
Lynch sees this as a deliberate attempt by Kurti to explain why Kosovo should now contribute to an international mission elsewhere, based on the argument that international forces helped provide security in Kosovo, and therefore Kosovo can now use its own experience and capabilities to assist another population.
Kosovo’s Security Forces have developed expertise in areas including search-and-rescue operations and demining, which policymakers in Pristina say could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
But the comparison between Kosovo and Gaza is also one of the most contested aspects of the decision because the circumstances surrounding NATO’s intervention in Kosovo and the proposed Gaza mission differ in fundamental ways.
In Kosovo, international intervention followed a war between Serbian forces and the Kosovo Albanian population and ultimately preceded Kosovo’s declaration of independence in 2008. Questions remain over whether Kosovo’s experience can straightforwardly serve as a model for the Gaza initiative. This distinction is important because Kurti’s comparison is not simply historical. It is also political.
Jelena Novakov, a Belgrade-based geopolitical analyst who writes for Kosovo Online, said the comparison is understandable given Kosovo’s own experience of conflict and international protection, but argued that it also contains a significant contradiction.
“For a young country that is still struggling with international recognition and, in a way, remains a recipient of international assistance through KFOR, this represents a significant demonstration of improved stability, even if largely symbolic,” she told The New Arab.
“What is debatable is the decision to participate in an initiative launched by the country that is largely responsible for the devastation in Gaza, after Kosovo itself experienced aggression,” Novakov added.
Dr Ilazi noted that Kosovo’s experience could provide a point of reference but cautioned against treating it as a model for Gaza.
“Kosovo and Gaza have different histories and political circumstances. Our experience cannot tell Palestinians what their future should look like. It can, however, remind us that people need both physical security and a say over how they are governed,” he said.
He also pointed to Kosovo’s own experience with international administration, arguing that this provided another lesson that could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
“We also know the frustrations of international administration, as we had our own share of that with [the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK)], and these include decisions made far from the people affected, unclear accountability, and arrangements described as temporary that become very difficult to change. That experience is worth sharing too,” Dr Ilazi said.
Kurti appears to be carefully framing his message to reassure Kosovar Albanians who may be uneasy about Kosovo’s involvement in Trump’s Gaza initiative. With 4,600 KFOR troops stationed in Kosovo, at least as of earlier this year, the southeastern European country continues to depend on international peacekeeping troops.
“Kurti is trying to say, ‘international peacekeeping troops have helped keep us safe, so now we can use our own unique expertise to help others.’ Kurti is also undoubtedly trying to communicate Kosovo’s unique value to Trump’s putative peace effort. Of course, all of this would be far more meaningful if Trump’s plan for Gaza actually benefited the people of Gaza the way NATO helped Kosovar Albanians,” Lynch explained to The New Arab.
"I would say this is the main problem with Kurti's framing: He’s right that international forces helped the [Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA)] force Serbian troops out of Kosovo in 1999. This was a prerequisite for Kosovo’s eventual declaration of independence in 2008. That’s the difference here,” she noted.
“By Kurti’s own analogy, what’s happening with Trump's Gaza peace plan is much more akin to what would have happened in 1999 if NATO troops had helped Serbia retain control of Kosovo and had helped Serbian forces keep Albanians in submission.”
By invoking Kosovo’s experience with international protection, the country’s prime minister is presenting participation in the ISF as an extension of a principle that Kosovars know personally, which is the idea that international forces can provide security to a population emerging from conflict.
Whether that principle applies to Gaza, however, remains a matter of significant disagreement.
Between Palestinian sympathy and strategic necessity
The decision is also likely to be viewed through the lens of Kosovo’s domestic politics. With many citizens of Kosovo sympathetic to Palestinians, there is tension between public sentiment and Pristina’s strategic interests.
Kosovars who oppose Trump’s Gaza plan or support the Palestinian cause may nevertheless view participation as a necessary cost of maintaining the United States as Kosovo’s closest ally, which can be understood as a limitation faced by a small state.
Novakov said, however, that the issue has so far generated little sustained public debate in Kosovo. She attributed this partly to the country’s wider political and economic problems, including prolonged political instability, inflation, stalled negotiations with Belgrade and the EU, deteriorating relations with Washington, and the legal proceedings involving former KLA leaders.
“There is currently no large-scale public conversation about this issue in Kosovo,” Novakov told The New Arab. “There is support for Palestine among Kosovars, but the government’s alignment with the US is rarely raised as one of the main issues during demonstrations.”
Dr Ilazi cautioned against assuming that political support for the deployment necessarily translates into broad public support for every aspect of the mission. Although he stated that the parliament’s 89-0 vote on 17 April to approve the government’s earlier decision to deploy Kosovo’s forces to the ISF “shows broad political support for participation,” Dr Ilazi stressed that it does “not tell us how the public will respond to every task the mission might undertake, and I would avoid claiming a public majority without reliable polling.”
As he explained, much will depend on what people see unfolding in Gaza.
“Clearing unexploded ordnance, helping aid reach families and making neighbourhoods safer are contributions the government can explain clearly. Public confidence would be harder to sustain if Kosovo’s soldiers became associated with restricting Palestinian movement or protecting arrangements that leave people displaced,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Kosovo has relatively little ability to influence major international conflicts and may therefore prioritise maintaining relationships with powerful allies, chiefly Washington. The result is a complicated political position in which criticism of the Gaza policy can coexist with acceptance of Kosovo’s participation, according to Lynch.
“The majority of Albanians are sympathetic to Palestinians, though there are some very vocal Zionist Albanians as well. But even those who support Palestine and deplore Trump’s Gaza plan are likely to accept the Kosovo government's decision to participate as a necessary cost of keeping America as their closest ally. The prevailing thought in Kosovo is ‘we’re a small country, there’s not much we can do to shape major world events and distant conflicts, so we will accept this arrangement because this is what our closest ally wants,’” she told The New Arab.
For Novakov, the calculation is ultimately rooted in Kosovo’s continuing reliance on international support. Around 100 countries have yet to recognise Kosovo’s independence, including five European Union members (Cyprus, Greece, Romania, Slovakia, and Spain), while Russia and China remain opposed to its statehood.
With Brussels’ focus increasingly shifting towards Ukraine, she argues, maintaining a close relationship with Washington remains particularly important for Pristina.
Questions over responsibility and accountability
Beyond public opinion, the deployment raises questions about legal and reputational responsibility. There are valid concerns to raise about the possibility that Kosovo’s involvement could expose its personnel or government to scrutiny if the wider operation were associated with forced displacement, the consolidation of Israeli control over Gaza, or other conduct that violates international law.
Lynch argues that these concerns deserve particular attention because of Kosovo’s own experience with international justice and accountability. The recent conviction and 25-year sentence of former Kosovo political and military leader Hashim Thaçi on war crimes charges has already placed questions of wartime responsibility at the centre of public debate.
Against that background, participation in a controversial international operation could create additional scrutiny if Kosovar personnel became associated with actions later determined to be unlawful.
Dr Ilazi distinguished between the legal and reputational risks Kosovo could face.
“I would also separate legal responsibility from reputational damage. Establishing legal responsibility requires evidence about particular actions and circumstances. Public trust can be lost much earlier if a mission is seen as facilitating abuse or denying Palestinians control over their future,” he told The New Arab.
He also argued that Kosovo should establish clear limits on what its personnel can be asked to do.
“Those restrictions need to shape operational planning, with legal review, reporting to the Assembly and a credible option to suspend or withdraw the contingent. We should not leave individual soldiers to resolve political ambiguities that their government failed to address,” commented Dr Ilazi, who also argued that the perspectives of Palestinians themselves should receive greater attention in discussions about the force.
“One issue that deserves more attention is how Palestinians themselves view the force. Most discussions focus on Washington’s intentions and the calculations of contributing countries. Yet the people expected to live alongside this mission need meaningful influence over the arrangements it supports. From Kosovo’s experience, we should understand how much that matters,” he argued.
A new test for Kosovo's foreign policy
Ultimately, Kosovo’s decision to participate in the Gaza stabilisation effort highlights the difficult choices facing a small state whose security and international standing have been closely connected to the United States for many years.
For Kurti’s government, participation offers an opportunity to demonstrate continued commitment to Washington and to portray Kosovo as a country capable of contributing to international security rather than simply receiving international assistance.
At the same time, the decision places Kosovo between competing pressures, including domestic sympathy for Palestinians, its strategic partnership with the United States, questions about the nature of the Gaza mission, and concerns about legal and reputational consequences.
As the deployment moves forward, the central question will be whether Kosovo can maintain its strong relationship with Washington while avoiding becoming entangled in the contentious political and legal disputes surrounding Gaza.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics.
Follow him on Twitter: @GiorgioCafiero
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Hamas harvests civilian casualties. The media should never be complicit - opinion
articles.body:
The rapturous reception for the documentary film NAZA, whose name comes from the Hebrew acronym applied to the collateral damage estimates carried out by all law-abiding militaries, has once again brought allegations of cruel and arbitrary slaughter of civilians to Israel’s door.
There is a noble assumption at the heart of conflict journalism: that unflinching reporting of the horrors of war protects civilians and holds military power to account.
But conflict has changed, the information battlefield has changed, and now the way civilian casualties are being reported is actually creating a strategic incentive to produce them.
This is a phenomenon called civilian casualty harvesting: the deliberate exploitation of civilian deaths and suffering as a military and political resource. It is related to human shielding, but it is not the same thing. It is a cynical and grotesque abuse of conflict reporting.
Human shielding describes the use of civilians to protect military infrastructure. International humanitarian law prohibits it. The International Committee of the Red Cross defines human shielding as using the presence or movement of civilians to render military objectives immune from attack or to shield or impede military operations.
Civilian casualty harvesting begins where human shielding ends.
Its purpose is not merely to make an enemy reluctant to shoot. It is to create a situation in which either decision benefits the exploiting belligerent.
Do not attack the military target, and the combatants survive.
Attack it, and civilians die, and their deaths become ammunition in another theater of war: phone screens, newspaper front pages, cinema, TV, international institutions, and Western public opinion.
The civilian has become strategically valuable precisely because he can die.
The NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence has described the strategic logic of human shielding in Gaza in strikingly similar terms:
“By engaging in these acts, Hamas employs a win-win scenario:
“If indeed the IDF uses kinetic power, and the number of civilian casualties surges, Hamas can use that as a weapon in the lawfare it conducts. It would be able to accuse the IDF (and Israel) of committing war crimes, which in turn could result in the imposition of a wide array of sanctions.
“On the other hand, if the IDF limits its use of military power in Gaza to avoid collateral damage, Hamas will be less vulnerable to Israeli attacks, and thereby able to protect its assets while continuing to fight.”
Cynical use of civilian casualties
The horrific innovation Hamas has perfected is the cynical use of civilian casualties to manipulate the global information environment.
A civilian death can now travel around the world before anyone knows what was targeted, whether combatants were present, what precautions were taken, who the dead were, or sometimes even what caused the explosion.
The image arrives first, context limps along after, and journalism, with its noble instincts drawing it toward human suffering, is allowing itself to be recruited into this twisted harvesting of death.
At CAMERA, much of our work consists of restoring context missing from reporting on conflict in the Middle East. Where were the combatants? What was the objective? Why is only violence from one side active, while the other is painted in passive and reactionary terms? This phenomenon is not restricted to any one outlet.
Hamas has learned that its strategy will not be questioned, and that the catastrophic suffering it causes to its own people will be uncritically amplified by Western journalists, driving public and institutional antipathy against Israel. It has identified an incentive structure.
If hiding among civilians makes you safer, you hide among civilians.
If preventing civilians from leaving makes enemy attacks politically more costly, preventing them from leaving becomes useful.
And if civilian deaths reliably generate international condemnation of your opponent, while scrutiny of your own role in placing civilians at risk disappears from the story, then civilian death has acquired strategic value.
This is where journalists and media outlets need to examine their own conduct. The failure is tiny and yet catastrophic. The simple fact is that by refusing to clearly label the original human shielding strategy, they have created an unending appetite for civilian death. Hamas has no reason to protect civilians in Gaza when putting them deliberately in harm’s way is so successful in achieving their war objective to isolate Israel on the world stage.
The journalist didn’t kill the civilian. The image didn’t kill the civilian. But an incentive doesn’t require direct responsibility; it requires participation and, darker still, complicity.
The war in Gaza has provided us with a stark case study in the harvesting of death for propaganda purposes, but it is by no means only an issue relating to Israelis and Palestinians. Western Europe arguably stands closer to the brink of war than it has since the 1930s. Iranian proxies across the Middle East hold huge populations captive. And in the digital era, the journalist, once the observer holding power to account, is now an active part of the battlefield.
Pressuring major outlets to acknowledge civilian casualty harvesting is not a hasbara (public diplomacy) issue. It is a reaction to the changed nature of conflict reporting in the era of the digital war. It is a campaign to prevent any civilian population from finding itself in the clutches of an authoritarian organization or government that realizes that civilians’ brutal deaths are more valuable to the war effort than their lives.
Crucially, acknowledgement would not ask journalists not to report on civilian deaths. The noble purpose remains the same. Report the deaths, but report clearly who caused them. If the BBC, for example, employed a simple formulation every time civilians died in Gaza because of Hamas strategy, “Hamas routinely embeds in civilian areas for strategic reasons,” it could, in nine words, strike a hammer blow to the incentive structure. If Hamas were being held to account for this horrific tactic, how long would the tactic remain useful?
The idea that being careful about context somehow diminishes compassion is backward and must be abandoned. The truth is more protective than ever. The media must fully commit to it, not just for the sake of Palestinians in Gaza, but for all of us.
The writer is a UK media researcher at CAMERA, the Committee for Accuracy in Middle East Reporting and Analysis. She previously founded Scotland Against Antisemitism.

articles.title: FM Sybiha: Dialogue with Iran was appropriate and useful for Ukraine’s strategic security
articles.body:
FM Sybiha: Dialogue with Iran was appropriate and useful for Ukraine’s strategic security
The head of Ukrainian diplomacy said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
According to the Minister, the meeting was a continuation of his July phone call with Araghchi, during which the sides agreed to maintain direct dialogue to prevent further escalation between Ukraine and Iran.
“Thanks to diplomacy, we managed to ease tensions and remove immediate threats at that time,” Sybiha said.
During the latest meeting, he said, the sides discussed the situation in Ukraine and Iran, regional issues, as well as peace efforts.
“Diplomacy is not just about meetings with friendly countries and photographs where everyone is smiling and embracing. Sometimes it is also about having a frank conversation with an ally of your enemy. We do not have to agree on everything in order to talk,” the Foreign Minister said.
He stressed that Ukraine supports direct dialogue even with states that maintain close relations with Russia.
“I believe the meeting was appropriate and useful, primarily in terms of Ukraine’s strategic security interests,” Sybiha emphasized.
As reported, on July 25, Iran accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, claiming that one sailor was killed and another wounded.
President Volodymyr Zelensky previously said that the Ukrainian Defense Forces had struck a warship and vessels involved in transporting military cargo from Iran in the Caspian Sea.
Later, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi “for a frank conversation.”
Following his conversation with Sybiha, Araghchi said that Kyiv should compensate Tehran for the damage caused by the attack.
In early August, Mohsen Rezaei, a senior military adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader, said that Tehran had been prepared to strike three targets in Ukraine, but abandoned the plans after allegedly receiving an “apology” from Kyiv.

articles.title: France ready to send troops to Ukraine immediately following ceasefire — radio report
articles.body:
PARIS, September 24. /TASS/. France is ready to deploy its military personnel to Ukraine immediately if a ceasefire is established there, the Europe 1 radio station reported.
The deployment of French soldiers could take place as part of the Coalition of the Willing to provide assistance to Kiev, it said.
The plan is to deploy French troops away from the front line at strategically important sites. "Their task will be to train, equip, and, above all, rebuild the Ukrainian army. Rafale fighter jets will help ensure airspace security," Europe 1 reported.
In addition to France, other countries in the Coalition of the Willing may also send troops to Ukraine. It is not yet known exactly how many soldiers these countries plan to send, but, according to the radio, the number could be in the thousands.
Russia opposes the presence of military personnel from NATO countries in Ukraine. Earlier, President Vladimir Putin stated that the deployment of European troops to Ukrainian territory would mean war with Russia.

articles.title: Four takeaways from Trump's summit with Xi in Washington
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Four takeaways from Trump's summit with Xi in Washington
US President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on trade and artificial intelligence and the growing strategic rivalry between the countries all in the spotlight during an elaborate state visit.
Here are some major takeaways from the talks:
TRADE DEAL EXTENDED, FOR NOW
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides had extended a trade truce that was due to expire in November during talks, but only by two months. He said the extension would give the two sides "more time to see what we can do on the economic front."
But rather than locking in a durable agreement, the extension appears to push the central questions — tariffs, Chinese purchases, rare-earth supplies and technology restrictions — into the next round of negotiations.
Bessent said on Wednesday that Beijing was meeting its requirement in the earlier agreement to buy 25 million tons of soybeans but was lagging on its pledge to buy $17 billion in other agricultural goods. US officials have said rare-earth deliveries were also falling short, another sign that significant gaps remain.
For companies, the result is a familiar form of instability: tariff rates remain lower for now, but decisions must still be made against a shifting policy backdrop.
Trump and Xi could have more opportunities to hammer out a more permanent deal ahead of the new January 10 deadline, with two multilateral summits scheduled in Shenzhen and Miami before the end of the year.
XI WANTS US 'PRUDENCE' OVER TAIWAN
As expected, Xi pressed Trump on the Taiwan issue, saying, according to China's official news agency Xinhua, that China hoped the United States would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence to lay a solid foundation for bilateral strategic cooperation and the development of China-US ties."
The agency's English-language service also wrote that Xi hoped the US would oppose Taiwan independence.
That would be a tougher version of Washington's long-standing formulation that it does not "support" independence. There are no signs that the Trump administration plans to change its wording.
There was no immediate White House readout of the exchange, but US officials have long avoided explicitly stating opposition to Taiwanese independence. Any shift in language would raise questions about Washington's resolve to defend the island and provoke opposition in Congress.
Washington is Taiwan's most important international backer and is bound by US law to provide it with the means to defend itself.
Trump raised questions about that commitment after his summit with Xi in May when he described a pending arms package for Taiwan worth up to $14 billion as a "negotiating chip."
STRATEGIC RISK
Xi, not for the first time while meeting Trump, invoked the "Thucydides Trap", an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one tends toward war.
While the Chinese leader said the risk "can be overcome," his reference underscored the extent to which concerns about a potential US-China military conflict continue to shadow relations between the world's two largest powers.
Xi argued that both nations stand to gain from cooperation and lose from confrontation, and he called for regular military dialogue and stronger crisis-prevention mechanisms.
Trump, for his part, drew on the two nations' shared history to emphasize the potential for cooperation. They could accomplish much by pursuing common interests, he said, invoking their wartime alliance against Japan.
DRESS TO IMPRESS
For Trump, Xi's White House visit was an opportunity to show off a Washington being remade in his image.
After Xi treated Trump in Beijing to a tour around a Ming dynasty temple and a walled-off garden retreat rarely opened to foreigners, the US president returned the favour with a different kind of spectacle: Troops wearing wigs and tri-corner hats marched in formation and played music in a Rose Garden redesigned to look like a Trump golf club.
Fighter jets and bombers roared overhead during ceremonies staged on Wednesday and Thursday, one so loud it caused Trump to flinch.
Trump has talked for months about needing more authority, often over the objection of courts and the US Congress, to beautify and remodel the nation’s capital ahead of Xi's visit, although many of the projects, like the new White House ballroom and the Reflecting Pool, are not yet finished or have run into problems.
When the White House press corps was called to cover the two leaders, it wasn’t to hear them talk about the weighty affairs of state. Instead, it was to watch them tour the Marine One helicopter and the recently redesigned South Lawn of the White House, replete with a large helipad emblazoned with the presidential seal.
Speaking to reporters, Trump brushed away questions about their policy discussions.
“He loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi. “Great meeting.”

articles.title: Defense official: Russia's neighbors have stepped up responses to air threats
articles.body:
Defense official: Russia's neighbors have stepped up responses to air threats
Due to Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine, more and more drones and even cruise missiles have ended up in neighboring countries, which is why the Baltic states and Poland have strengthened measures for responding to air threats, said Gert Kaju, head of the Ministry of Defense's defense readiness department.
The side effects of Russia's aggression are increasingly being felt in countries adjacent to the war zone; for example, 39 drones have entered Moldovan airspace this year, Kaju said on Friday at the weekly briefing held at the Ministry of Defense.
"In addition, drones have been shot down in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and also Romania. And Russian cruise missiles have also ended up in third countries — they have either flown through that airspace or somehow veered into it," he described.
"In response to this, the procedure for deploying air‑defense assets has been made faster, primarily in Poland and also in the direction of the Baltic states — meaning the chain of command has been simplified and accelerated in order to respond to this air threat," Kaju said.
According to the overview presented by the Ministry of Defense representative, Russia continues long‑range strikes on Ukraine's critical infrastructure, hitting residential buildings, industrial enterprises, administrative buildings and transport infrastructure in at least 14 oblasts over the past week.
"According to Ukrainian data, Russia has launched circa 1,900 jet‑powered drones in September, of which Ukraine claims to have destroyed circa 60 percent," he noted. "Due to these attacks, Ukraine has lost nearly 90 percent of its steel‑production capacity."
Ukrainian strikes against energy infrastructure
With its long‑range strikes, Ukraine hit oil‑refining plants in various Russian regions during the previous week of the war, including in Moscow, Yaroslavl and Samara oblasts. As a result of the strikes, Russia's oil‑refining capacity has suffered additional losses; Russia is losing production capacity, Kaju said.
"In addition to infrastructure related to oil refining, Ukraine continues to strike Russia's logistics centers, including in the Moscow region," Kaju added. "As for medium‑range strikes, here Ukraine's drone units have focused primarily on airfields in Crimea and Rostov oblast, as well as areas related to drone storage and launch sites, and also additional energy facilities in Crimea."
According to Kahju, more than 400 different energy facilities in Crimea have been hit since early July, and in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea Ukraine has managed to put more than 300 vessels out of action.
Fighting continues in Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblasts
Speaking about what is happening on the front line, Kaju said that the most intense fighting is still taking place in Donetsk oblast, in the direction of Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka, as well as in the direction of Lyman. Following these in intensity are Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv oblast.
Ukraine has carried out counterattacks primarily in Kharkiv oblast, including in the direction of Kupiansk, and in Donetsk oblast, where Ukraine's focus is primarily on the Lyman direction.
"Russia's combat losses are 1,500 soldiers per day, and therefore we can say that Russia's weekly losses are over ten thousand soldiers," Kaju stated.
Russia's threats and propaganda continue
Kaju also spoke about how Russia continues rhetoric in which it blames everyone else for what is happening in Ukraine, including Ukraine and the Western world, with Moscow claiming that the Western world is using this situation to generally escalate relations with Russia.
"Russia also continues pressuring countries that support Ukraine, so that they would abandon supporting Ukraine," he said. "As an example, we can point out the situation where the Russian Foreign Ministry summoned the chargé d'affaires of the United Kingdom in Moscow and issued an official protest against London's further increase of arms deliveries to Ukraine. At the political and communicative level, Russia continues to spread its worn‑out narrative," Kaju described.
"In addition to the fighting and the air threat described above in neighboring countries, hybrid activity has increasingly come into view in third countries — whether direct acts of sabotage, various types of information operations or other such activity. That is, companies involved in supporting Ukraine are threatened, attempts are made to attack them or force them to stop their activities," the Ministry of Defense official said.
"All of this is part of Russia's narrative, where their goal is to create fear and uncertainty on the other side, because creating fear and uncertainty is one part of Russia's deterrence policy, trying through this to show that Russia is a large and threatening force," he explained.
"Our response to this must be, on the one hand, that we monitor it, respond to these steps with our own steps, and in the case of incidents it is also important to attribute the event to its initiator," Kaju emphasized.
"So in summary — one thing is the war in Ukraine, but on the other hand its effects are increasingly felt in neighboring countries, primarily through the hybrid activities described above. Our task is to monitor and respond to them according to the nature of the threat," Kaju said.
--
Editor: Mait Ots, Argo Ideon

articles.title: Russia makes revolution in jet-powered UAVs — newspaper
articles.body:
LONDON, September 24. /TASS/. Russia has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution, The Guardian reported.
According to the publication, "since May there has been a notable set of upgrades, allowing Russian forces to strike Ukraine more effectively with fast, jet-engined drones."
The Guardian also noted that the new models of Russian Geran drones are faster than the Ukrainian interceptors.
Earlier, the Financial Times and Reuters reported that the new drones reach high speeds and fly at high altitudes, blurring the line between drones and cruise missiles.

articles.title: Zelenskyy shared details of the Drone Deal
articles.body:
Zelenskyy shared details of the Drone Deal
Kyiv • UNN
As part of the Drone Deal, Ukraine will share with its partners its experience in using drones and protecting critical infrastructure. The initiative also includes joint production.
The bilateral Drone Deal agreements provide not only for the sale of drones and missiles, but also for the exchange of experience between Ukraine and partner countries. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this while speaking with journalists, UNN reports.
Details
According to Zelenskyy, Russia will continue hybrid attacks against various different countries.
First of all, Russia will continue hybrid attacks against various countries, and not only NATO members. We are seeing hybrid attacks, as well as drone attacks, against Moldova, which is neither a NATO nor a European Union member. There are attacks against Germany, there is Romania, and so on
Answering a question about whether Ukraine would provide support to such countries in the use of drones, he added that within the framework of the Drone Deal, Ukraine and its partners could share experience in using drones and protecting critical infrastructure.
We have offered our assistance to various countries, certainly first and foremost to the countries that are helping us during the war. The countries know about this. By the way, the Drone Deal, when we talk about this document, is bilateral—it does not depend on whether a country is a NATO member or not a NATO member. The main thing is that it is our partner. So, when we sign the Drone Deal, it is not only about the sale of drones or missiles, but also about an exchange of experience. And what you are talking about is precisely part of this exchange of experience. How we sent our specialists to the Middle East, how we helped protect critical infrastructure
We remind you
Ukraine is inviting international partners to join the Drone Deal Initiative, which provides not only for the procurement of unmanned aerial vehicles, but also for joint production and the development of defense cooperation.

articles.title: Last Warthog Departs Nellis as Base’s A-10 Era Comes to a Close
articles.body:
Nellis Air Force Base, Nev.—a longtime hub for A-10 Thunderbolt II tactical training, operational testing and maintenance—ended nearly a half-century of flying the venerable Warthog on Sept. 22.
The Air Force said in a Sept. 23 statement that nearly 70 Airmen lined up on the flightline at Nellis for a final salute as the last Warthog there took off.
Nellis has flown A-10s since 1977. The base has been the Air Force’s primary proving ground for A-10 tactical employment, and units have worked to refine its software, avionics and precision weapons, the Air Force said.
The 66th Weapons Squadron at Nellis’ U.S. Air Force Weapons School has also trained more than 300 A-10 weapons officers in 100 classes, the Air Force said.
With its heavy armor and withering GAU-8 30mm cannon, the A-10 was originally built to be a Soviet tank killer and played a central role in the Gulf War against Saddam Hussein’s army. But in the Global War on Terror, the A-10 became best known as a reliable close air support platform to defend U.S. and partner nations’ ground troops when they were besieged by insurgents.
The A-10 also carries out a close air support mission dubbed Sandy during combat search and rescue operations, most recently in April during the successful rescue of two F-15E air crew who were shot down in Iran.
For years, though, the Air Force has tried to retire its A-10 fleet amid concerns that it would not be survivable against an advanced enemy. Congressional opposition has thwarted those plans before, but that has softened in recent years.
The service had pressed to retire all 162 of its remaining A-10s by the end of fiscal 2026, but after the Iran war began and the rescue of the F-15E crew, the Pentagon announced it would delay at least some Warthogs’ retirement until at least 2030.
Still, the fleet and its accompanying enterprise are slowly winding down. Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona, another longtime A-10 hub, graduated its last class of new Warthog pilots in April and held its farewell flights for its last aircraft in July. The maintenance depot for the A-10, at Hill Air Force Base, Utah, also closed this year.
The Air Force stressed that while the A-10 is retiring, the service will not let its close air support capability fade.
“Foundational tactical expertise, operational roles and personnel are transitioning to multirole and advanced fighter platforms across the service,” the Air Force said in its statement.
The F-35, for example, is taking on CAS and combat search-and-rescue roles, the service said, taking advantage of its fifth-generation stealth capabilities, advanced sensor suites, and secure data-sharing networks to carry out precision ground support missions in contested environments.
The 66th is working to teach pilots of other fighters how to take on the Warthog’s traditional missions, squadron commander Lt. Col. Ridge Flick said. The unit will also keep training combat rescue officers, pararescue Airmen, special tactics officers, and combat controllers, he said.
“We are maintaining the culture of the A-10 by involving as many other fighter communities involved in the close air support mission,” Flick said in the statement. “We are also training F-15 Eagle, F-35 Lightning II and F-16 Fighting Falcon pilots to take on some roles we have had in combat search and rescue.”
Airmen who used to repair and sustain A-10s at Nellos as part of the 757th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron’s Thunder Aircraft Maintenance Unit are being reassigned to other squadrons and airframes like the F-35 and F-16, the statement said.
“The discipline that A-10 maintainers developed over 50 years of managing airframe fatigue, wing replacements and depot-level overhauls is being integrated into those newer flight line programs,” the Air Force said.

articles.title: Inside the bunker: How a Zelensky aide struggled to explain away corruption
articles.body:
Inside the bunker: How a Zelensky aide struggled to explain away corruption
A senior official in Vladimir Zelensky’s office frantically tried to reconcile her official annual salary of $12,500 with what surveillance records suggest was $30,000 per month in cash payments received from her new boss, a former head of Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR), according to a new investigation.
In records published by veteran investigative journalist Vladimir Boyko, Irina Mudraya, a former deputy justice minister serving as deputy head of Zelensky’s office, allegedly confided in her property magnate accomplice: “Who will ever believe me that I live on 50,000 hryvnia [$1,100] a month? Who?”
Mudraya was fired in August after being accused of laundering millions through Ukraine’s banking system to bail out one of Zelensky’s energy ministers, who himself had been arrested in a separate case involving the Ukrainian leader’s long-time associate Timur Mindich.
Boyko has been publishing pages of what he says are transcripts of surveillance recordings produced by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) between January and June as detectives followed Mudraya and her partner, former MP Maksim Mikitas.
Who is tasked with countering corruption in Kiev?
NABU and its sister agency, the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), established after the armed coup of 2014, have repeatedly clashed with Zelensky’s cabal. Last year, the Ukrainian leader attempted to place them under his control, but reversed course after Western donors threatened to suspend all aid.
Most recently the agencies exposed a massive scam-call center protection racket that was run through the office of Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who then fled abroad under the false pretense of attending a conference in Paris.
Earlier this month, HUR agents engaged in a gunfight in Kiev with agents from the rival Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), which some news outlets linked to the fight for protection money from the scam-call criminal businesses.
Aside from NABU and SAPO, the National Agency on Corruption Prevention (NAPK) obliges hundreds of thousands of civil servants to submit annual finance and property declarations.
What did Mudraya have to worry about, according to the transcripts?
According to the transcripts, Mudraya received some $30,000 a month in cash payments from a man she called “Kirill Alekseyevich.”
Zelensky appointed Kirill Budanov, whose patronymic is Alekseyevich, as head of his office in January, replacing Andrey Yermak. Yermak resigned last year as initial news broke of Zelensky insiders syphoning some $100 million through energy contracts.
Mudraya appeared to seek advice from her partner Mitkas on hiding her ill-gotten riches from NAPK.
“You can declare the Bvlgaris and at least the Van Cleef. But no way can you declare the earrings,” the man said. “I’ll put you in touch with a man who will handle the income issue.”
Buying a Van Cleef piece during the war with Russia was “f**ked up,” Mudraya admitted.
The exchanges, which Boyko has staked his reputation on, suggest senior officials were flying under NAPK’s radar.
Mudraya and Mikitas discussed securing a highly paid sinecure that could cover for her enormous under-the-table income. She mentioned her envy of Zelensky’s adviser on sanctions policy, Vladislav Vlasyuk, who she said officially earned $335,000 a year as a member of the oversight committee of state-owned Sense Bank.
Sense Bank is the former Ukrainian branch of Alfa Bank, nationalized in 2023 under Kiev’s anti-Russian sanctions and through which Mudraya allegedly laundered cash by having the bank’s anti-fraud team suspend their digital monitoring platform.
While Mudraya said netting a job like Vlasyuk’s would not be legally possible, Mikitas suggested that a teaching position at a private institution could serve the same purpose. He offered to speak to a friend who headed a construction university, but Mudraya said she would look ridiculous teaching anything other than law.
Does the corruption link reach upwards?
According to the recording, Mudraya’s new boss personally delivered her first “salary,” unlike his predecessor who had a “specially trained girl” to carry cash. The payout turned out to be larger than expected:
“It was 30 [thousand dollars]. I went to him and said: ‘Kirill, it’s too much.’ Brought the hat with me. He says: ‘You said 30.’ I say: ‘No, I said I used to get 30. But we agreed to 20, not 30.’ He said: ‘Well, I won’t take it back.’”
Subsequent transcripts suggest the higher monthly payments continued and that Mudraya received an additional $20,000 bonus in May.
“He values you a lot,” Mikitas concluded. “Mark my word, in two months you’ll become first deputy prime minister,” he added, saying he expected “Kirill” to become the new cabinet chair.
What could the leaks mean for Budanov?
Some Ukrainian media have argued that NABU is targeting Zelensky’s inner circle to leverage reforms demanded by the EU.
Bloomberg reported that European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had a “tense meeting” with Zelensky this week, conditioning further financial support on implementing the changes Kiev had promised to Brussels.
Reform would give more power to NABU and SAPO and introduce oversight by EU-aligned experts for appointments of senior officials, curbing Zelensky’s extensive influence and the corrupt network he runs through his inner circle.
NABU and SAPO accused Yermak of involvement in a major money-laundering scheme in May and leaks to pro-EU media implicated Zelensky himself.
No formal charges can be filed against Zelensky as long as he holds presidential powers, which he has attempted to retain under martial law since his term expired in 2024.
Replacing Zelensky’s personal friend Yermak with Budanov, who has extensive contacts among Western special services, seems to be consistent with the EU’s goals.

articles.title: Iran still not seeking to obtain nuclear weapons — president
articles.body:
NEW YORK, September 25. /TASS/. Iran still has no intention of obtaining a nuclear weapon, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Fox News in an interview.
When asked whether his country had any desire to acquire a nuclear warhead, he said: "Absolutely no."
"Our martyred revered Supreme Leader [Ali Khamenei] said several times in the past that this is religiously forbidden. From the religious standpoint, it is prohibited to have a weapon of mass destruction," he added.
He reaffirmed his country’s readiness to observe the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
"We have never sought to obtain a nuclear weapon. We want to comply with the Non-Proliferation Treaty," the Iranian president said.
In his words, Iran is ready for agreements with the United States, and is putting forward demands only within the framework of the international law.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Russian Electronics Plant Supplying Parts for Kh-59 Missiles and Pantsir-S1
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Russian Electronics Plant Supplying Parts for Kh-59 Missiles and Pantsir-S1
A Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s Ulyanovsk targeted the NPP Zavod Iskra electronics plant, which supplies products to the Russian defense industry, according to an OSINT analysis by independent Russian media outlet ASTRA.
An ASTRA OSINT analyst identified the affected facility as JSC NPP Zavod Iskra in Ulyanovsk. The plant is part of Russia’s Almaz-Antey aerospace and defense corporation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ulyanovsk regional Governor Alexey Russkikh confirmed that industrial and civilian infrastructure in the city had been damaged in the drone attack.
According to preliminary information provided by Russkikh, eight people were injured, including seven adults and one child. Five of the adults were reported to be in moderate condition, while the remaining two sustained minor injuries. The child was also described as being in moderate condition.
Founded in 1971, Zavod Iskra is a major Russian electronics manufacturer specializing in the development and serial production of semiconductor devices, microwave components, power electronics, medical products, and LTCC ceramic packages for electronic equipment.
According to Militarnyi, Zavod Iskra is also part of the supply chain for Kh-59M2/M2A guided air-launched missiles. The company provides the Yaroslavl Radio Plant with 3OT127A transistor pairs used to manufacture SB-1AM television transmitters for T1A-02 equipment.
It also supplies diodes used in the TVK-2 television channel of the 72V6 combat vehicle, a component of Russia’s Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile and gun system.
The reported strike in Ulyanovsk came as another major Russian industrial facility was targeted by drones. The LUKOIL-Permnefteorgsintez refinery, one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, was also hit in a drone attack on September 25, ASTRA reported, citing an OSINT assessment.
Perm regional Governor Dmitry Makhonin confirmed a drone attack in the region and said emergency services had been deployed to the site.
