The US has supplied about a third of Europe’s diesel imports this year, with its share rising to around half in August, according to government data. Prices at the pump have already reached record highs in Germany and the Netherlands.
Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said Brussels was monitoring the markets and security of supply “very, very closely,” noting that the US was a “major supplier” of both diesel and liquefied natural gas as part of the bloc’s “diversification strategy since 2022.”
Trump backed the idea of restricting exports on Tuesday as US diesel prices hit a record $6.52 a gallon ($1.72 per liter). “I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” he told reporters ahead of a meeting with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky.
Trump has also repeatedly urged Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, saying the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage.
The issue was raised during talks between Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in New York on Wednesday. According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, Lavrov said Ukrainian attacks on energy and cross-border infrastructure were deliberately contributing to instability in global energy markets.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to stabilize its domestic market. The measures run through January, although direct producers have been permitted to export diesel, marine fuel and gasoline since September.
Supplies have also been squeezed by the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that normally carries around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Gulf diesel and gasoline exports fell to just over a quarter of pre-war levels in August, according to the International Energy Agency.
The EU has sharply reduced purchases of Russian energy since the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Russia’s share of the bloc’s gas imports plunged from 45% to 12% by 2025, while its share of oil imports dropped from 27% to about 2%.
Moscow has blamed the EU’s decision to cut Russian energy imports as a key factor behind the crisis. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said last week that Europe was facing “the worst energy crisis in history,” describing the situation as “self-made.”

articles.title: Xi calls for constructive China-US relationship
articles.body:
President Xi Jinping told Donald Trump on Thursday that Beijing and Washington must peacefully manage their superpower rivalry, as the US president gave his Chinese counterpart a lavish welcome to the White House.
In his opening remarks with Trump, Xi said the two countries must ensure there is "no conflict and no confrontation between us."
Xi also warned that the development of artificial intelligence should be "always under human control" – in contrast to Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed warnings that AI could threaten humanity itself.
Trump, for his part, emphasised his "truly great friendship" with Xi.
"President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries," he said after greeting Xi for his first visit to the White House in over a decade.
Xi said the two countries' interests were deeply intertwined and that competition between them should be a "healthy one." US companies were welcome in China, he said, adding that he hopes "Chinese companies are treated fairly here in the United States."
A readout from Xinhua news agency after the two leaders met in the Oval Office quoted Xi as saying that the two sides need to work toward a relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, while moderating competition and managing differences with promises of peace.
The president also said a new trade arrangement between the two superpowers was good news for industries and people of both countries, as well as the global economy. 
As long as the two sides uphold the spirit of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit, a way out of problems can be found, Xi said.
On AI, Xi said while China and US are competitors as major powers in the field, they have even more reason to cooperate. He called for continued dialogue to exchange views on its risks and benefits, and to work together to prevent the misuse and abuse of the technology.
Xinhua cited Xi as saying that the two sides should maintain "human control" over Ai technologies, and ensure that AI serves human progress.
He also urged Washington to adhere to the correct position of opposing "Taiwan independence" and handle the Taiwan question with caution, so as to lay a solid foundation for China-US strategic cooperation.
On Iran, Xi urged Trump to end the Mideast war "through negotiation as soon as possible," after the American leader forcefully defended his use of military power in a speech at the UN earlier this week, suggesting he could "annihilate" Iran.
Following their remarks on Thursday, the two leaders observed a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden. After their closed-door meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House's South Lawn.
"He loves good granite," Trump told reporters, adding that the two men had a "great meeting" without elaborating. (Xinhua and agencies)
Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: Trump and Xi Meet Ahead of State Dinner With Top A.I. Leaders
articles.body:
Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad.
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

articles.title: WATCH: Netanyahu poised to speak at UN General Assembly, address Iran war, nuclear program
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the genocide claim against Israel was "the lie of the century, while adding that the Iranian regime's toppling was "only a matter of time," during his Thursday address to the United Nations General Assembly.
One of the main topics in Netanyahu's speech was the different fronts that the country is fighting, with the prime minister explaining that Israel is also fighting on the information front against countries that push for antisemitic narratives and spread lies "such as the genocide claim."
"What genocidal regime gives millions of polio vaccines to the enemy population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of two million tons of food to Gaza, a ton per person?" Netanyahu asked the assembly, adding that a majority of the fighting was done in the social media sphere.
Netanyahu also said that there were several countries in the region actively financing information campaigns against Israel, with Qatar being the first one to hold these sorts of policies and Turkey being the last one.
"Years ago, Qatar started financing universities and the toxic media outlet Al Jazeera. They did the same in Europe, by the way. And their goal was clear. Brainwash young minds to hate Israel, America, and the West. This is the same Qatar that holds the Hamas butchers of October 7," he said.
"Now the last country to become an antisemitic spreader of lies is Turkey. [Turkish President Recep Tayip] Erdogan is a tyrant who also hosts the Hamas terror chiefs," he added.
Netanyahu also explained that the Turkish leader has "murdered thousands of Kurdish civilians, denies the Armenian genocide, has jailed thousands of journalists, and in fact, he holds the world record for this, and illegally occupies northern Cyprus and regularly trespasses into Greece, a NATO member."
He said that it was no surprise that now Erdogan was "attempting to trespass into Syria, and that's not surprising. Because he called for Israel's destruction almost every single day. He says he is going to be the ruler of Jerusalem. No sir, you won't."
Netanyahu calls out Mamdani for links to Hamas, Hasan Piker
During his speech, Netanyahu also called out to recently elected New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani for his policy, saying that Jews are worried about the state of the city and the safety. "Many tell me that this is not the New York that we know, and that they can't believe how fast it changed," he pointed out.
"It's no wonder if we consider that you [Mamdani] praised criminals convicted of supporting Hamas; you count as friends people like Hassan Piker, who said America deserved 9/11. Some friends you have. You invite into your home a Palestinian journalist who filmed Hamas terrorists beating and torturing Israeli hostages and later admitted that he refused to publish the videos in order to protect the terrorists. Your wife likes a post praising the Oct. 7 massacre, and another saying Tel Aviv shouldn't exist," Netanyahu added.
"Mr. Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here; you tried to silence me. Well, you can silence me, you can't silence the truth," the Prime Minister continued, and said: "And here is the simple truth: Israel didn't commit genocide; Israel prevented genocide. And that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done if we hadn't stopped them; they would have killed every last one of us."
Netanyahu refers to West Bank violence, recounts latest attacks against Israelis
In another moment of his speech, Netanyahu recounted the recent rise in West Bank violence, saying that the settler population can't be represented by 150 youngsters who "throw rocks and burn down olive trees."
"I can't stand for vigilantes, and that's why we are looking for them with the Shin Bet," he continued, adding that there is no comparison between settler violence and the terror attack perpetrated by Palestinians against Israeli civilians in the West Bank.
"Three days ago, an Israeli-French citizen was shot by a Hamas terrorist in a lake in Judea and Samaria. Two days ago, a reservist was run over by a terrorist while in Judea and Samaria," he recounted, then explaining that the victim of the car ramming was Neria Leiter, an American citizen who serves as an IDF reservist and is the son of Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter.
"In a recent post, before he was attacked, Neria wrote this: We have no country; it is a privilege to defend it. To Neira, and to all the heroes of Israel, I pledge: Your sacrifice won't be in vain. We will continue to fight and to win, because we have no other choice," Netanyahu said.
Starlink, beepers, and people leaving during his entrance
During the speech, Netanyahu also used prompts to explain his points, starting by showing a beeper when recounting how the IDF destroyed the Hezbollah threat with the beeper operation, and also a Starlink antenna receptor when speaking about the Iranian people rising up against the regime.
While talking about Iran, Netanyahu also recalled how the protests seen against Israel in Gaza and the West Bank were not seen when Iran repressed protesters in the streets. "But I have news for you. In Iran, the power of the people will overcome the people in power," he said.
During Netanyahu's address, several delegations walked out and booed the Prime Minister when he was called to the podium. Although several delegations left the plenum, 120 remained in their seats, according to the Prime Minister's Office, which told Walla.
Additionally, Iran's delegation left a photograph of arch-terrorist Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force leader Qasem Soleimani on the bench.
Bennett, Golan, Sa'ar react to Netanyahu's speech
Former prime minister and B'Yachad party leader Naftali Bennett said that Netanyahu missed his "historic opportunity to declare Qatar an enemy and expose its involvement in the October 7 massacre to the entire world."
"In doing so, he whitewashes and legitimizes Qatar. Every moment Netanyahu refuses to call the Qatari enemy by its name harms our national security, damages Israel's standing in the world, and dishonors the memory of those murdered in the massacre," Bennett added.
"Qatar is an enemy with the blood of our people on its hands. They funded [Hamas's] Nukhba forces, celebrated the massacre, have hosted and continue to host Hamas leaders, and even at this very moment, continue to spread antisemitic propaganda worldwide calling for Israel's destruction," he continued.
"Netanyahu speaks about Hamas, but he is trying to hide the truth. Without Qatar, there is no Hamas. Netanyahu is handing Qatar the keys to Gaza, which is why he has been unable to defeat Hamas for three years now," the former prime minister said.
"We will declare Qatar an enemy, oust it from Israel and Gaza, and defeat Hamas," Bennett concluded.
Netanyahu's speech "presented our truth in the house of lies that is the UN," Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said.
"Israel's prime minister must be equipped with the abilities and skills to fight for Israel's cause and to be a player on the international stage. The candidates seeking to replace Netanyahu in these elections do not have these abilities that Netanyahu has," Sa'ar added.
"I was surprised to hear that Netanyahu is accusing Qatar of spreading lies and hosting Hamas leaders on October 7. Apparently the speech did not align with Yonatan Urich," Democrats party head Yair Golan said.
Danon, allied nations presidents meet with Netanyahu on the sidelines
Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, welcomed Netanyahu and his wife Sara before the PM took the stage.
Protests were reported outside the UN Headquarters against Netanyahu's presence at the gathering of world leaders.
Several protesters were arrested by the New York Police Department for causing disruptions outside UN HQ.
Among those arrested was anti-Zionist movie star Susan Sarandon, Walla learned.
Before his speech, Netanyahu met with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis on the sidelines of the UNGA.
Netanyahu "emphasized the importance of the strategic partnership between the countries for regional stability and welcomed Greece's selection of Israeli defense systems," the Prime Minister's Office said.
Netanyahu and Mitsotakis discussed "regional developments, energy cooperation, and the advancement of another tripartite summit with Cyprus," the PMO added.
Netanyahu also met with Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša on the UNGA sidelines, the PMO confirmed.
He thanked Janša for the opening of the Israeli embassy in Ljubljana and his "steadfast support for Israel, which has led to a turnaround in bilateral relations," the PMO said.
The two leaders "discussed opportunities to deepen cooperation between the two countries in various fields," and Netanyahu invited Janša to visit Israel, the PMO noted.

articles.title: Eight attempted suicides during US aircraft carrier's extended mission
articles.body:
Eight attempted suicides during US aircraft carrier's extended mission
WASHINGTON, Sept 24 - There were eight suicide attempts among US sailors on board the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during its extended 286 consecutive-day deployment at sea, the Pentagon told a lawmaker in a written response to questions.
The nuclear-powered Lincoln, with roughly 5,000 personnel, was involved in the US naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran and — according to Democratic lawmakers — set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea. The strike group consists of the carrier itself and several other warships.
In a letter to US Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand dated September 22, Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao said that while there were no suicides during the deployments, there were a total of eight attempts on board the aircraft carrier and its accompanying vessels.
It was unclear how many individuals carried out the attempts.
"That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable," said Gillibrand, who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
Earlier this month the Abraham Lincoln and some of its supporting ships arrived at port in eastern Thailand after 286 days at sea, after having been deployed last November.
Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months but can be extended during times of conflict. Mental health issues on long deployments have long plagued the US Navy. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran offers Trump deal before US election
articles.body:
Iran offers Trump deal before US election
Iran has offered the US a new deal aimed at ending the months-long conflict before the midterm election in November, directly challenging President Donald Trump’s claim that Tehran is deliberately waiting until after the election to reach an agreement.
Trump claimed in a speech at the UN on Tuesday that Iran is deliberately stalling the talks to see how Republicans perform in the November 3 midterm election, and predicted that Tehran would make a deal “right after” the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if negotiations fail.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told reporters on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Thursday. “We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” he said, referring to the memorandum of understanding reached by the US and Iran in June.
“We did reach an agreement with your president… The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialogue, descended into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway,” Pezeshkian said in an interview with Fox News. “We will stand resolutely to defend ourselves. We never sought war… It’s America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran has submitted a proposal in which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within around a week and negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program rapidly resumed. The proposal was sent through mediators during talks in New York this week.
Under the plan, Tehran would restore navigation through the crucial oil shipping route in exchange for Washington lifting its economic blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, and releasing some frozen Iranian assets. Iran is also seeking an end to hostilities on other fronts, including Israel’s combat operations in Lebanon.
US and Iranian negotiators are discussing a phased arrangement in which the blockade and restrictions on Hormuz would be addressed first, Reuters reported, citing Iranian, regional, and Western diplomatic sources.
Tehran has not abandoned its claim to regulate Hormuz, with Iranian officials continuing to insist that the waterway should be managed by Iran and Oman and that fees should be charged for services provided to passing vessels.
Araghchi said the proposal largely follows the terms of the June memorandum rather than introducing new demands, adding that Iran is waiting for a response.
Araghchi has also held a series of meetings with foreign counterparts in New York, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Moscow has said there is “no alternative” to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the “illegal actions” of the US and Israel.
The renewed diplomatic push comes amid mounting pressure on both sides. The US blockade has sharply restricted Iran’s oil exports, while Tehran’s controls over Hormuz have disrupted one of the world’s most important energy corridors and helped push oil prices above $100 a barrel and US diesel prices to historic highs.
Pezeshkian, who is the first foreign head of state to speak at the UN while his country is at war with the US, told the chamber on Wednesday that Tehran is prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but will not negotiate under threats of force and “will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”

articles.title: NAZA to stream free after Israel threats against filmmakers
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
NAZA Gaza film to stream free after Israel threats against directors
Award-winning documentary NAZA will stream online for free following its worldwide release in November, giving audiences around the world access to the film about Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
NAZA, directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, will be released in cinemas in more than 50 countries before streaming on the website of British newspaper The Guardian in November.
Announcing the decision on X on Thursday, Abraham said the documentary would be made available for free because of its "interest and public importance".
"…I and Rachel decided together with The Guardian that the film NAZA would be accessible online for free, without any time limit, so that every person can watch it and the soldiers' testimonies," Abraham wrote on X.
The Guardian said the film would be streamed "as part of the news organisation's commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism".
The film, shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, centres on Israel's use of AI in its genocidal war on Gaza, featuring testimony from 24 members of the Israeli military and intelligence services who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Its title comes from an Israeli military term used to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
The soldiers and intelligence personnel interviewed describe systems used to identify targets in Gaza and how strikes were approved despite the anticipated deaths of civilians, including children.
The documentary received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere at the Venice Film Festival in September and went on to win the Special Jury Prize.
But the film's reception in Israel was markedly different, triggering a fierce campaign against Abraham and Szor from senior Israeli politicians, military figures and far-right activists.
Much of the backlash centred on the film's use of testimony from serving and former Israeli military and intelligence personnel to expose the systems behind attacks that have killed Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
Israeli officials accused the filmmakers of portraying Israeli soldiers as war criminals, while Culture Minister Miki Zohar accused them of "treason against the state". Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir threatened to use "every tool at our disposal" against it.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to pass legislation that would allow authorities to strip citizenship from Israelis who "smear" soldiers or "defame" the state.
The campaign soon extended beyond the filmmakers themselves to their families.
Dozens of far-right activists gathered outside the homes of the directors' families, including the home of Szor's parents, after messages circulated calling on activists to demonstrate there.
Some messages included explicit calls for violence, while one protester demanded the "death penalty for traitors" and called for the homes of the filmmakers' families to be demolished.
The threats prompted expressions of solidarity from Israeli human rights groups and members of the international film industry, who condemned the campaign against the directors and called for their safety and freedom of expression to be protected.
In 2025, Abraham and Szor won the Oscar for Best Documentary for No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal.
That film, which documented Israeli settler violence and the displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, also generated controversy in Israel.
Following the Oscar win, Ballal was brutally attacked by Israeli settlers.

articles.title: Iran to strongly respond to new US attacks: Pezeshkian warns
articles.body:
He made the remarks in an interview with Fox News’ Bret Baier on Thursday, highlighting, “We never initiated a war, but if they [US] wish to keep fighting with us, we will respond strongly and resolutely.”
The interview was conducted on the sidelines of his trip to New York for participating in the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
He said Iran has been forced to defend itself whenever it has come under attack.
Pezeshkian also rejected pressure aimed at forcing Iran to surrender outside the framework of the international law.
“And today the pressures that they keep imposing on us are to force us to surrender outside the legal framework of international law, which is impossible.”
The remarks come against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began with air raids on February 28, which assassinated a number of high-ranking Iranian officials and military commanders, along with more than 160 schoolchildren and staff in Minab.
The war came to a temporary halt after 40 days, following Iran’s mighty response to the aggressors. Tehran and Washington then signed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding on June 17 to end the war. However, the US breached its commitments and ignited more rounds of fighting as the MoU collapsed.
“Without any legal justification or framework, they attacked us, assassinated our Leader, our scientists are military commanders, government officials, and our children,” Pezeshkian said.
He said the United States had labeled Iran as terrorists while Iran had been the target of terrorism.
Asked about indirect negotiations between Iranian diplomats and US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in New York, Pezeshkian said Iran's position remained anchored in international law.
“That which is discussed and negotiated is within the framework of international law, and what would be rightfully ours under international law.”
He said Tehran had never sought anything beyond its lawful rights. “We never sought anything more, and the result of that, based on that foundation, we're seeking an agreement if the counterpart agrees to it.”
Pezeshkian noted that Tehran is “willing” to move forward with the Islamabad MoU
Pezeshkian said the central obstacle in negotiations with the US was the “deep mistrust” that has developed between the sides.
He linked that mistrust to the fate of the 2015 nuclear agreement, saying Iran had previously reached an agreement with the United States before Trump withdrew from it unilaterally in May 2018. “Your president tore that up.”
Pezeshkian questioned how the two sides could resolve outstanding disputes if they could not establish trust through dialogue.
“If we're unable to trust one another within the framework of a dialogue, how can we hope that these issues will ever be resolvable?”
President Pezeshkian noted that the Strait of Hormuz was fully open before the start of the terrorist US-Israeli aggression on Iran.
He said that the restrictions imposed by Iran over the strategic energy chokepoint were a response to the aggression and also the illegal blockade imposed by the US against Iranian vessels.
“The problem is that within the strait, those who have been responsible for a lifetime for a strait, they are forbidden to move their vessels through the waterway; then of course, we will not recognize that right for other vessels.”
MNA

articles.title: Poland probes second healthcare cyberattack as FM warns Russia may be planning ‘something big’
articles.body:
A cyberattack on a Polish healthcare software provider compromised the confidentiality of patients’ personal data, a treatment centre said, weeks after a separate breach exposed records belonging to nearly 19 million people, local media reported on Friday.
The latest attack targeted Qbusoft, the company behind Medyc software used by healthcare providers to manage patient records, Polish broadcaster TVP World reported.
The Rehabilitation and Psychiatric Treatment Centre in Inowroclaw said on Thursday that patients’ contact details and national identification numbers may have been affected. It did not specify how many patients were involved.
Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the Central Office for Combating Cybercrime was examining the incident as part of a broader investigation. He said the government had issued new security recommendations to companies supplying software to the healthcare sector.
“In the event of a breach of any security procedure by a private company, strict consequences will be imposed,” Gawkowski said.
The incident follows an August breach involving MyDr, a system used by about 12,000 healthcare providers. Data belonging to almost 19 million people, including information on medicines and prescriptions, was exposed in that attack.
Polish FM warns Russia may be preparing ‘something big’ this year
Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has warned that Russia may be preparing a major operation this year and could stage a false-flag attack to justify further mobilisation.
“We are receiving information ... we are not revealing the sources, but there are many (of them), that Russia is preparing something big this year,” Sikorski said at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on Thursday, according to Polish broadcaster TVP World.
“I believe that Putin needs a pretext for mobilisation, so they could carry out a false-flag attack and tell the Russian people: ‘We are under attack, and therefore we need to mobilise,’ ” he added.
Sikorski did not specify what the reported operation might involve. Asked about possible scenarios, he said Belarusians were concerned about being drawn into the war in Ukraine.
He also warned that Baltic countries with Russian minorities could face escalation, saying NATO must be ready to deter potential aggression.
A full-scale Russian invasion of a NATO member would be “crazy,” he said, suggesting that Moscow might instead pursue a less explicit action that would make it harder for the alliance to invoke its Article 5 mutual-defence clause.

articles.title: Flamingo engines storage facility, Ukrainian logistics sites: results of Russian strikes
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces continued to strike military-industrial complex facilities and logistics centers, as well as naval vessels operating on behalf of the Ukrainian armed forces over the past night, the Defense Ministry reported.
TASS has compiled the key information on the results of the strikes.
Defense Ministry’s statement
- The Russian Armed Forces continued to carry out strikes against military-industrial complex facilities and logistics centers, as well as naval vessels operating on behalf of the Ukrainian military, the ministry emphasized.
Targets of strikes
- According to the Defense Ministry, as a result, a Fire Point facility for the storage and assembly of unmanned aerial vehicles in Borispol in the Kiev Region was hit on whose premises Honeywell TFE731 engines to power Flamingo long-range cruise missiles were stored.
- Russian forces also struck two logistics centers in Odessa and the town of Nerubaiskoye, which were used to store and distribute military and dual-use cargo delivered to Ukraine from European countries.
- In addition, mooring infrastructure and three storage facilities with military equipment were hit in the port of Reni in the Odessa Region.
- The Russian Armed Forces also struck a bulk carrier carrying military supplies and dual-use cargo for the Ukrainian army at sea.
Situation in Ukraine
- A piece of railway infrastructure was damaged in the Poltava region in northeastern Ukraine, regional administration head Vitaly Dyakovnich reported.
- Infrastructure was also damaged in Krivoy Rog in the Dnepropetrovsk Region in southeastern Ukraine, Alexander Vilkul, head of the city’s defense council, wrote on his Telegram channel.
- Transport infrastructure facilities were damaged in the Zhitomir region in northern Ukraine, regional administration head Vitaliy Bunechko noted.
- According to information published on his Telegram channel, fires broke out at the sites.
- The number of damaged facilities has not been specified.

articles.title: US backs Musk’s X in legal battle with EU
articles.body:
US backs Musk’s X in legal battle with EU
The US government has joined Elon Musk’s appeal against an EU fine imposed on X, accusing Brussels of “regulatory overreach” and escalating a transatlantic clash over its regulation of US tech firms.
The European Commission fined X €120 million ($136.51 million) for alleged violations of its 2022 Digital Services Act, the first such penalty under the bloc’s Digital Services Act (DSA), a vast legislative censorship and media control apparatus. Brussels accused the platform of breaching rules on transparency, advertising, and data access, as well as using a deceptive blue-tick system for verified accounts.
Musk, who has claimed the EU’s tech regulations stall technological progress and equated the bloc to a “Fourth Reich” over them, appealed the decision in February, seeking to overturn the fine.
On Thursday, the US Department of Justice said it had filed an application to intervene in support of Musk’s legal challenge.
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within its jurisdiction,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said. “We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory over-reach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth.”
🚨 United States Files Request to Intervene in Case Brought by X Corp. and Elon Musk Seeking to Annul Decision by European Commission
“The European Commission inappropriately attempted to expand its regulatory authority to reach American companies not present or operating within…
The Justice Department warned that the case – the first DSA enforcement challenge to reach the General Court – could set a precedent for US tech firms. Citing “significant concerns” over Brussels’ approach to liability and jurisdiction, it said Washington has an interest in “protecting American companies from foreign extraterritorial enforcement action.”
Separately, the EU is investigating X for other potential DSA breaches, including its approach to content moderation and explicit images generated by its Grok AI chatbot. Under the DSA, the EU has also probed Meta Platforms and Amazon, while Apple was fined under a sister law, the Digital Markets Act, over alleged anti-competitive behavior in its App Store. Apple is appealing a €500 million fine under the regulation.
Neither the European Commission nor X responded to media requests for comment on the US intervention.
US-EU clash over Big Tech
EU scrutiny of US tech firms has become a major source of friction between Brussels and the administration of President Donald Trump, which has backed claims that the bloc unfairly targets American tech giants and harms digital free speech. Senior administration figures, including Vice President J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have criticized the EU’s fine on X as an attack on American companies. Musk previously accused the EU of trying to shut down X, claiming in 2024 that the commission had offered him an “illegal secret deal” to “quietly censor speech” to avoid a fine.
Trump has railed against the X fine, calling it “nasty” and warning that “Europe is going in some bad direction.” He has strongly condemned the DSA and related tech regulations, repeatedly labeling them “overseas extortion” and a “form of taxation.” He has threatened new tariffs on European goods unless the EU rolls back the regulatory penalties. The European Commission has rejected Trump’s criticism, insisting the DSA is non-discriminatory and applies equally to all large tech platforms operating in Europe.
DSA: Online safety or censorship?
Brussels sells the DSA as an online-safety law meant to fight illegal content and “disinformation.” Critics see something far more sinister: an expanding censorship and narrative-control regime that gives unelected EU officials sweeping leverage over political speech – and over the largely American tech platforms that carry it.
That criticism gained ammunition from a 2026 report by Republicans on the US House Judiciary Committee.
They have accused the bloc of a “clear bias” toward censoring conservative and populist parties, pointing to its intervention in Romania’s election, then in Hungary, where arch EU critic Viktor Orban was heavily defeated by pro-EU Peter Magyar. It also cited pressure on platforms in Slovakia, the Netherlands, France, Moldova, and Ireland, as well as at EU level.
Brussels has also gone beyond pressuring platforms. The EU banned RT and Sputnik in 2022 and has sought tighter controls on what it considers Russian disinformation, and has since pushed platforms to clamp down on what Brussels labels Russian disinformation. The commission itself admitted DSA-linked mechanisms are being used to address Ukraine-related content and election risks. Critics argue that, backed by the threat of massive fines, the system gives Brussels powerful leverage over narratives that challenge its political and foreign-policy consensus.
That leaves a stark divide over what Brussels’ flagship internet law actually does. The EU calls it online safety; its critics see a censorship architecture capable of suppressing dissenting narratives, shaping the information environment around elections, and forcing global tech platforms to police political speech on Brussels’ terms.

articles.title: ArcelorMittal closes Ukraine's largest steel plant after Russian attacks
articles.body:
ArcelorMittal closes Ukraine's largest steel plant after Russian attacks
The company said this on its website, Ukrinform reports.
The company noted that Over the past five weeks, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has been targeted by four missile strikes, resulting in fatalities, injuries and extensive damage to production facilities. The most recent attack occurred on September 21.
In total, the four attacks claimed five lives and injured 17 employees, one of whom remains in a critical condition.
"ArcelorMittal has with deep regret advised the Government of Ukraine that it is unable to restart operations at its Ukrainian subsidiary in a safe and sustainable manner," the company said in a statement.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo noted that since the start of the full-scale war, the company's employees in Ukraine had worked tirelessly to keep the mines and steel plant operating.
"We are discussing the future of the plant with the Government of Ukraine and will focus on preserving the infrastructure, so when peace finally returns, options for restarting production remain available," he added.
ArcelorMittal also noted that the workforce of ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih had demonstrated extraordinary resilience throughout the full-scale war.
The company provided financial support to ensure the continued operation of ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, allocating more than $700 million to the enterprise.
At the same time, ArcelorMittal expects to record a non-cash impairment charge of approximately $1 billion, principally reflecting the impairment of property, plant and equipment at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih.
In May, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih shut down a blast furnace, two sintering machines and an ore beneficiation plant due to disruptions to logistics, citing inadequate services provided by Ukrzaliznytsia as the reason. Ukrzaliznytsia called the statement blackmail.
Photo: Archive

articles.title: ‘Flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food’ – Nepal PM mocks world system
articles.body:
‘Flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food’ – Nepal PM mocks world system
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah has slammed the current global system, saying it allows weapons to be moved efficiently but leaves poorer countries struggling to secure food, fuel, and other essentials for their populations. 
“We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food,” Shah told the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday. 
The rapper-turned-politician pointed to the shortages his country has faced amid conflicts and geopolitical tensions disrupting supply chains, saying farmers have struggled to obtain fertilizer, road projects lacked bitumen, and families faced shortages of cooking fuel. 
“Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline,” Shah, who was elected to Nepal’s top job earlier this year following ‘Gen Z’ protests against corruption, told the assembled world leaders. “But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.”
📹 'Hit By Climate We Didn't Warm, Hit By Wars We Didn't Start': Nepal PM Balen Shah's Rousing Speech At UN
"This is not Nepal's private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. Ask Pakistan. Ask any other country in our region and you'll hear the… https://t.co/e4U0xT14i1pic.twitter.com/5Bi4Qwi26M
He argued that the problem extends beyond his country, specifically pointing to India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, the Maldives, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka as regional states facing pressures from climate shocks and conflicts.
Nepal is recovering from catastrophic flash floods that were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Tibetan border on August 26. The wall of water, mud, and rock tore through mountain communities, killing at least 1,400 people and leaving more than 6,000 missing. Nepal estimates its physical recovery needs at around 10% of its gross domestic product.
The prime minister described the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster as a “warning to the world,” saying a warming climate is destabilizing the Himalayan ecology and increasing the risks of avalanches, floods, and landslides. The devastation affected both sides of the Nepal-China border before floodwaters continued downstream toward India.
Shah also proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India, and China. The initiative would involve sharing satellite data and technical expertise, monitoring dangerous glacial lakes, strengthening joint early-warning systems, and coordinating assistance when disasters cross borders.
India and China were among the countries Shah thanked for providing what he called “prompt and generous assistance” after the floods.
The Nepalese leader also called for greater grant-based support for countries rebuilding after climate disasters, arguing that recovery should not force poorer states to take on additional debt. He said Nepal is not seeking to blame individual countries, but wants greater international responsibility and a more equitable global system

articles.title: US, Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz, end US blockade
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US and Iran discuss phased deal to reopen Hormuz and end US blockade, sources say
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
"One way forward would be to solve the crisis in stages. The first would be to end the blockade and reopen Hormuz," he said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
That would involve US President Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix, after an earlier understanding collapsed in July. So a central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Trump has said he thinks the US and Iran could reach a deal after midterm elections to Congress on November 3. A senior European official said the Iranians "have a very long list of demands."
A White House official said that while "Iran is desperate for a deal, President Trump holds all the cards and will make whatever decision is best for the United States."
Trump, he said, remained "open to talking with Iran under the right circumstances" but had no need to negotiate, and the US was in a "very strong position" with control of the Strait of Hormuz and an Iranian economy that was "collapsing."
The official said "crushing sanctions" and "one of the most successful blockades in history" have crippled Iran’s economy and left Iran completely broke. Trump was content to let the "inevitable Iranian collapse" play out rather than be "played" by Tehran, the official said.
Former US negotiator Dennis Ross said he saw only a 30% chance of an agreement being reached before the vote, but that both sides may have stronger reasons to make a deal before than after the midterms.
"The blockade is what's really squeezing the Iranians. It's strangling them," Ross said.
A deal before the midterms could benefit Trump, as reopening Hormuz could ease tensions in the Gulf, contain oil prices and help bring down politically sensitive US gasoline prices.
Iran's chances of gaining much-needed economic relief may be greater while Trump still has a greater political incentive to strike a bargain.
After the midterms, Ross said, Trump may face fewer constraints and be more willing to intensify pressure or consider military options.
LEVERAGE AS OBSTACLE?
The leverage that brought Washington and Tehran back to negotiations could also make compromise harder.
Washington controls the pressure that is hurting Tehran most, while Tehran controls access to a critical energy chokepoint. Neither side wants to surrender that leverage without extracting something tangible in return.
This means the midterms may be less a deadline for diplomacy than for preserving the conditions that make the diplomatic efforts possible. If Washington and Tehran cannot turn leverage into a deal before the midterms, the diplomatic window could narrow as the risk of escalation grows.
Even as it seeks a diplomatic off-ramp, Tehran is preparing for the possibility of renewed war with Washington, the Iranian official said, accusing the US of using the economic blockade and threat of force as tools of coercion.
"Our fingers are on the trigger,” said the senior Iranian official. “The Americans know what they need to do but, because of their excessive demands, the chances of diplomacy resolving this are extremely low.”
Regional sources said Tehran was willing to drop a demand for payment of transit fees to use the Strait of Hormuz from the main agreement and put the demand in a side attachment instead, as ending the blockade had become the more urgent priority.
Gulf states have rejected the proposal for payment of transit fees. Any arrangement would be temporary, not a formal abandonment of Iran’s position, the regional sources said.
The US has tightened the economic vice on Iran, layering new sanctions on top of a blockade that has choked off Iran's oil exports, an important source of hard currency.
This month, it targeted Iran's remaining commercial airlines and support networks as part of a campaign to sever the economic lifelines sustaining the government and the powerful Revolutionary Guards. Trump warned that Iran's economy could "rot" unless it reached a deal.
"Iran is not primarily focused on imposing tolls in Hormuz but on preserving its administrative control of the waterway,” he said. "Iran may be willing to defer the toll issue, but they are not going to give up administrative control of the strait.”
At the heart of the diplomacy in New York is a fundamental tension. Washington wants pressure to produce concessions, Tehran wants pressure removed before making them, and the Gulf states want the conflict resolved without allowing the region's strategic waterways to become enduring bargaining chips.
FEARS OF AN OPEN-ENDED CONFLICT
During a separate meeting with Trump in New York, Gulf leaders sought clarity on Washington's endgame beyond the midterms, including on whether the US would resume military action if Iran refused to return to negotiations.
They conveyed their collective rejection of any Iranian control of Hormuz, saying freedom of navigation must be restored and that the strategic waterway should not become a tool of coercion against Gulf states, regional sources said.
Yet alongside their warnings over Hormuz, Gulf leaders have pressed hard for de-escalation and a political process, reflecting the region's determination to stay out of any further conflict between the US and Iran.
"It's still not clear what Trump’s endgame is, or what the alternative to the pressure campaign would be," said Ebtessam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Center think tank based in Abu Dhabi.
"The Iranians, by contrast, know what they want. They're reshaping the regional landscape through Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb with a clear objective while Washington has yet to define its roadmap," she said, referring to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
That uncertainty is also shaping Tehran’s calculations. Danny Citrinowicz, a regional analyst and former Israeli military intelligence officer, said the New York talks had not altered the basic positions of either side and that Iran was unlikely to retreat as long as it believed Trump wanted to avoid a wider escalation before the midterms.
“The blockade is hurting them, but rather than softening their position, it is likely to drive them to escalate because they believe that if they soften their position, they are dead," said Alan Eyre, a former US negotiator on Iran.
A Western official familiar with the talks added: "It is all about opening the Strait of Hormuz. We're all under pressure domestically and the Iranians know that."

articles.title: French-Lebanese man sues over Israel uprooting 600 olive trees
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
French-Lebanese man files legal complaint over Israel's uprooting of 600 olive trees
A French businessman of Lebanese origin has filed a legal complaint against unknown individuals over alleged war crimes, accusing the Israeli military of uprooting 600 centuries-old olive trees owned by his family, his lawyers told AFP on Wednesday.
The 37-year-old Frenchman, who has not been publicly named, said in the complaint that some of the trees were up to 500 years old and had been uprooted from land cultivated by his family for 250 years in the village of Zawtar al-Sharqiya, his birthplace in southern Lebanon.
According to the civil complaint, filed over theft, destruction and damage to property that it alleges amount to war crimes, the trees were uprooted from the ground.
The plaintiff, who states in his complaint that he is "not a member or supporter of Hezbollah" – the armed group fighting Israel – said he suspects the trees were transported to Israel. The complaint adds: "There is no evidence to indicate that Hezbollah was using the house or agricultural fields for military purposes".
Israel has often claimed that its attacks in southern Lebanon, Beirut’s southern suburbs or other parts of the country are targeting Hezbollah bases and operatives. Close to 9,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Lebanon since the conflict erupted in October 2023.
According to the plaintiff, a digital entrepreneur, his family home was completely destroyed in an Israeli airstrike just hours before a ceasefire was announced in southern Lebanon in April 2026.
He said that the Israeli army took full control of his village a few weeks later, followed by the uprooting of the olive trees, after Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement in late June, which Israel has failed to uphold.
The complaint argues that "the destruction and uprooting of olive trees is evidence of war crimes committed by Israel in southern Lebanon," citing in particular a report by Amnesty International.
"These events are part of a broader context of ethnic cleansing and the destruction of numerous villages by Israel in southern Lebanon. Our client expects the French justice system to do everything in its power to identify those responsible and bring them to justice," his lawyers told AFP.
Lebanese officials, NGOs and local residents have condemned the systematic destruction of farmland, particularly through burning, by Israel in southern Lebanon.
The Israeli military has used white phosphorus, banned under international law.
Southern Lebanon is home to a significant share of Lebanon’s olive groves, an important part of the country’s agricultural sector, which has been significantly impacted by the war.
Since invading Lebanon in October 2024, just a year after the start of hostilities with Hezbollah, Israel has widened its occupation to include large swathes of the south along the entire border.
Dozens of towns and villages have been razed or largely devastated in the so-called "Yellow Line," a security zone established by the Israeli military which it says is to push Hezbollah back from the border.
Despite a lull in fighting since the June agreement, Israeli attacks have continued across the south, including home demolitions.
Other complaints have been filed in Paris against the Israeli military over alleged war crimes in Lebanon, including one brought by French-Lebanese artist Ali Cherri, who lost his parents in an Israeli airstrike on a residential building in Beirut in April, and another filed in July by a French-Lebanese man who lost his mother, sister and two nephews in Israeli airstrikes.
Israel conducted more than 100 strikes in 10 minutes on Beirut and across Lebanon on 8 April, a day after the US-Iran ceasefire was announced, massacring more than 350 people in what has become locally known as 'Black Wednesday'.
Israel has refused to leave Lebanon before Hezbollah is fully disarmed, but the Iran-backed group has refused to surrender its weapons as long as the occupation continues.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says shot down 6 ballistic missiles launched by Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi-led coalition says shot down 6 ballistic missiles launched by Houthis
Yemen’s Houthis said they targeted a ‘sensitive’ site in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis say they have intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Iran-allied group towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
The missiles were destroyed on Thursday in the direction of the Saudi cities of Taif and the strategically important port of Yanbu, according to Major General Turki al-Malki, the spokesman for the Saudi-backed Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Yemeni government in military and diplomatic push to reverse Houthi gains
- list 2 of 3As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
- list 3 of 3Yemeni forces say they repel Houthi attacks in Taiz as fighting rages
Saudi air defences intercepted some of the missiles attempting to target the cities, Al-Malki told the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
Hours later, Yemen’s Houthis said they had launched missile and drone attacks on what they described as “a sensitive target” in Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
The attacks came as the Reuters news agency reported that an air defence system operated by Greek military personnel in Saudi Arabia intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone on Thursday in the wider Yanbu region, home to major oil refining facilities.
“Both were shot down,” a Greek security source told Reuters, adding that the Greek Patriot system launched two missiles but did not give details on the origin of the drone and the ballistic missile. A second source confirmed the information to the news agency.
Yanbu port is key to Saudi crude when shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted.
Earlier on Thursday, Saudi Arabia’s General Directorate of Civil Defence issued alerts warning of potential danger in the holy city of Mecca, the northwestern area of Tabuk, the Red Sea areas of Jeddah and Yanbu and the southern area of Taif. They later said the threat had passed and the cities were out of danger.
Last week, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Mecca, an accusation the group strongly denied, with Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi calling the Saudi claims “a heinous lie”.
It was the first time in nearly 10 years that a security alert had been activated in Mecca, home to the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest site.
The Houthis have largely attacked southern areas of Saudi Arabia.
They stepped up attacks on the kingdom after declaring a naval blockade in July, a second theatre for the US-Iran war. The Houthis also seized the whole of Yemen’s western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
Forces with Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government said on Thursday they repelled Houthi attacks along several fronts in Yemen’s southwestern Taiz governorate.
Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, said that the Houthis launched coordinated attacks on Wednesday night in a bid to reach positions on a key road connecting the Aden, Lahj and Taiz governorates.

articles.title: South Korea slams ‘callous and irresponsible’ Zelensky
articles.body:
South Korea slams ‘callous and irresponsible’ Zelensky
Vladimir Zelensky put his personal interests first when he breached an agreement with Seoul not to disclose the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war captured in Russia, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has said.
Zelensky touted the arrangement during his speech to the UN General Assembly this week, saying it was “not easy to capture alive” the two soldiers. North Korea deployed troops to assist Russia in repelling a Ukrainian incursion into Russia’s Kursk Region in 2024-2025.
Lee rebuked Zelensky, without naming him, in an X post on Thursday, arguing that statesmen should put national interests first rather than opportunistically seeking to boost their own popularity.
The Ukrainian leader demonstrated a “callous and irresponsible attitude [that is] simply unacceptable,” the president wrote, stressing that Seoul and Kiev had agreed to keep the highly sensitive transfer private.
South Korean opposition lawmaker Yoo Yong-won, who championed the transfer of North Korean POWs since meeting them in Ukraine last year, told reporters that the two soldiers arrived in the country earlier this week.
He criticized the Lee administration for seeking to keep the agreement with Zelensky secret and said the government “should have taken a more proactive and assertive approach.” The deal was reached sometime in June, he added.
Kiev has long pressured Seoul to provide direct military support for the conflict with Russia, citing North Korea’s involvement in the conflict. Yoo said that, as far as he knew, the delivery of the POWs was not conditioned on South Korea changing its policy of not sending weapons to Ukraine.
South Korea does not formally recognize the government in Pyongyang as legitimate and considers all Koreans citizens of a single nation, regardless of the part of the peninsula where they were born.
The two soldiers captured in Russia are said to have expressed the wish to be sent to South Korea. Both were reportedly taken prisoner in January 2025.

articles.title: Swedish, Finnish fighter jets intercept group of Russian military aircraft
articles.body:
Swedish, Finnish fighter jets intercept group of Russian military aircraft
STOCKHOLM, Sept 25 - Finland and Sweden said on Friday they had scrambled fighter jets to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland, in the first such joint operation by the two Nordic countries.
The Baltic Sea region, of which the Gulf of Finland is part, is on high alert after incidents involving gas pipeline outages, airspace violations and drone sightings since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said the operation, which took place on Thursday, showed how the so-called Quick Reaction Alert cooperation could monitor and safeguard both countries' airspace.
"It is a concrete expression of the readiness and trust we have built together – and an expression of the strength in the Nordic, Nordic-Baltic, and broader NATO cooperation in our part of the world," Kristersson wrote in a post on social media X.
"The Baltic Sea has never been as vulnerable as it is now – but it has also never been better protected than it is right now," he said.
The two air forces' jets tracked down and identified a group of Russian aircraft including a transport plane and several fighter jets, the Finnish Air Force said.
The Russian embassies in Stockholm and Helsinki did not immediately respond to requests for comment when contacted by Reuters.
Finland and Sweden both joined NATO following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, departing from a longstanding policy of non-alignment. Their Nordic neighbours Norway, Iceland and Denmark were already members of the Atlantic alliance, as were the three Baltic republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. REUTERS

articles.title: New nuke sub leaves yard and heads to Scotland for trials
articles.body:
Cumbria Police closed Michaelson Road Bridge in Barrow-in-Furness on Thursday morning, working in collaboration with BAE Systems, and told residents a further message would be published once the crossing reopened.
The force confirmed the closure at 9am and said the bridge would remain shut while the operation was carried out. An updated statement issued later said: “Michaelson Road Bridge has now reopened. Thank you for your patience.” The closure ran until around 11.40am.
The UK Defence Journal understands that the operation covered the departure of a submarine from the yard, and that the boat involved was HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of the Astute class, with people gathering along the dockside to watch her leave.
Agamemnon was commissioned into the Royal Navy on 22 September last year at a ceremony in Devonshire Dock Hall attended by the King. Around 500 guests were present, and on the same day the King conferred Royal Port status on the town while steel was cut for HMS King George VI, the fourth and final Dreadnought-class submarine.
She completed a three-day trim dive shortly after commissioning, submerging to around 15 metres to confirm the integrity of the pressure hull and to establish her centre of gravity, with crew and engineers moving 16 tonnes of lead weights around the boat to simulate different loading conditions.
Steel was cut for Agamemnon in July 2013 and she was launched in October 2024, making her construction the longest of any nuclear submarine built for the Royal Navy, a delay attributed variously to the pandemic, the diversion of resources to begin the Dreadnought programme and the complexity of the Astute design.
Michaelson Road Bridge carries traffic across the entrance to Devonshire Dock, and closures of this kind are a familiar feature of submarine movements at the yard, with the bridge having to be swung clear before a boat of that size can pass out into Walney Channel.
At 7,400 tonnes and 97 metres, the Astute class carries Spearfish heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk Block IV land attack missiles, and the boats protect the deterrent submarines and the carrier strike group while also conducting surveillance and intelligence work. Seven were ordered, with the final submarine still under construction in the same hall.
Barrow remains the only facility in the United Kingdom with the infrastructure, site licence and resources to design and build British nuclear submarines, and the Defence Nuclear Enterprise annual update to Parliament published this month recorded that the workforce there has grown by more than 1,800 under the current government.
The yard is also preparing for the programmes that follow, with steel due to be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS submarine in 2027 and the concept design completed earlier this year for SMITE2, a new submarine propulsion testing facility at the site.

articles.title: Civilians are bearing brunt of Yemen fighting: UN rights chief
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN rights chief says civilians are bearing the brunt of fighting in Yemen
Civilians are being hardest hit by surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, the UN human rights chief said on Thursday.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement, without giving a breakdown of who was responsible for the casualties.
A total of 125 people were documented by his office as killed or wounded in the latest flareup in the conflict. Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
The statement said the UN human rights office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi movement, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
It was not immediately clear if the UN toll included any deaths or injuries from those incidents.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities.
He cited what he said was the targeting of inmates at a correctional facility in al-Hazm in al-Jawf province, as well as homes and schools in several areas. He said the UN allegations were false and unsupported by evidence.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi Arabia's diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Lavrov, UN nuclear watchdog chief discuss Zaporizhzhia plant, Iran nuclear program
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov discussed the situation at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and Iran’s nuclear program with International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi during a meeting in New York, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Thursday.
The ministry said in a statement that the meeting took place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and focused on what it described as “ongoing Ukrainian attacks and provocations” against the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant and the nearby city of Enerhodar.
The situation surrounding Iran’s nuclear program following strikes by Israel and the US on Iranian nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards was also on the agenda, it said.
Lavrov also met UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with the two officials exchanging views on international and regional issues, particularly the situation in the Gulf and the Palestinian territories.
The Russian foreign minister also held talks with Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, discussing bilateral relations and the results of a recent meeting of the Russian-Jordanian intergovernmental commission, as well as the escalation in the Middle East, including the Palestinian-Israeli conflict.
Lavrov met separately with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic to discuss bilateral cooperation and the political situation in Serbia and the Balkans, including the Kosovo settlement based on UN Security Council Resolution 1244.
He also held talks with Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye on strengthening bilateral ties, including trade, investment and humanitarian cooperation, as well as international and regional issues and coordination on multilateral platforms.
The Russian foreign minister also met the foreign ministers of Brazil, Algeria, Trinidad and Tobago, Nicaragua and Lebanon, as well as Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy and Swiss Foreign Minister and Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) Chair-in-Office Ignazio Cassis.
The discussions covered bilateral cooperation and coordination at international organizations, as well as regional and international issues, including the Middle East, the situation in Lebanon and the work of the OSCE and the UN, the ministry said.

articles.title: Polish foreign minister warns Russia may be preparing ‘something big’ this year
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has warned that Russia may be preparing a major operation this year and could stage a false-flag attack to justify further mobilization.
“We are receiving information ... we are not revealing the sources, but there are many (of them), that Russia is preparing something big this year,” Sikorski said at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on Thursday, according to Polish broadcaster TVP World.
“I believe that Putin needs a pretext for mobilization, so they could carry out a false-flag attack and tell the Russian people: ‘We are under attack, and therefore we need to mobilize,’ ” he added.
Sikorski did not specify what the reported operation might involve. Asked about possible scenarios, he said Belarusians were concerned about being drawn into the war in Ukraine.
He also warned that Baltic countries with Russian minorities could face escalation, saying NATO must be ready to deter potential aggression. A full-scale Russian invasion of a NATO member would be “crazy,” he said, suggesting that Moscow might instead pursue a less explicit action that would make it harder for the alliance to invoke its Article 5 mutual-defense clause.
Sikorski said Russia could sustain its war in Ukraine for another year or two despite economic pressure, unless Ukrainian strikes destroy more than half of its oil refinery capacity.

articles.title: EU to discuss who will give up their place in queue for Patriot missiles to Ukraine – source
articles.body:
EU to discuss who will give up their place in queue for Patriot missiles to Ukraine – source
Defence ministers of EU member states will discuss on 28 September in Brussels the possibility of giving up their place in the "queue" to purchase Patriot interceptor missiles from American manufacturer Lockheed.
Source: European Pravda, citing an unnamed EU official
Details: According to the source, the EU will hold discussions on planning the supply of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine.
EU member states understand that Ukraine needs interceptors "as soon as possible", European Pravda source said.
They said some of the Patriot missiles will be provided directly by the United States under the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme, which supplies Ukraine with US-made weapons.
"Another portion could be provided if states agree to swap their orders with Ukraine," the senior official said. He pointed out that the Council of the EU meeting of defence ministers on 28 September "will be another opportunity to press member states on this".
Update: Another source in the EU institutions said discussions are also under way on the possibility of an EU member state transferring Patriot interceptor missiles it already has to Ukraine, with Ukraine then using funds from the €90 billion loan to order the same number of missiles from the manufacturer in the United States for that country.
According to European Pravda sources, the country in question could be Spain or Greece.
Background:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that during his meeting with Donald Trump in New York, the US president told him that he had decided to grant Ukraine licences to produce missiles for Patriot air defence systems.
- Zelenskyy announced earlier an agreement on a package of Patriot missiles with one state, whose name has not been disclosed.
