articles.title: Trump praises US-China friendship at state dinner with Xi Jinping
articles.body:
Trump praises US-China friendship at state dinner with Xi Jinping
The two superpowers seek greater dialogue despite differences over issues such as Iran, Taiwan, AI and trade.
United States President Donald Trump has thrown China’s leader Xi Jinping a state dinner featuring a tech-heavy guest list, as well as a number of billionaires, Washington powerbrokers, business leaders and the type of festivities that most excite Trump, who has a reputation for reveling in hosting parties.
The dinner on Thursday night wrapped up a day of talks between the two leaders. The summit, Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade, is the second meeting this year between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.
Earlier on Thursday, Trump touted what he described as a “great meeting” with Xi, as the two superpowers seek greater dialogue despite differences over issues such as Iran, Taiwan, AI and trade.
“President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” Trump said during his toast on Thursday night, The Associated Press news agency reported.
“Together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations,” Trump added.
Trump has done his best to impress Xi during the Chinese leader’s three-day visit to Washington, and the US president praised their close personal relationship — even as he has decried top Democratic candidates as “communists” ahead of the November midterm elections.
Xi and Trump discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence during business hours, all while a First Amendment fight over press access at the White House was unfolding. But Trump publicly chose to focus on showing Xi his White House updates on Thursday afternoon, including letting him tour his Marine One presidential helicopter and a new helipad he built for it, before attention quickly turned to the flashy details of the swanky meal.
At one point, Trump invited dinner guests to tour the site of the new ballroom he is building nearby. Construction projects are a frequent digression for a president who has put a lot of focus on remaking Washington’s physical infrastructure.
Xi noted in his own toast that “President Trump has pledged to make America great again” and that “China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation”.
“These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing,” Xi said.
Those who attended included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and French luxury goods company LVMH CEO Bernard Arnault.
The dinner came after the president took the unusual step of personally greeting Xi and his wife on Wednesday as they arrived at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington. Normally, presidents wait for their guests to arrive at the White House itself before offering a formal welcome.

articles.title: As Trump hosts Xi, China reiterates call for dialogue to end Iran war
articles.body:
Riyaz ul Khaliq
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Beijing Thursday reiterated its call for a peaceful end to the Iran war as US President Donald Trump was set to host Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“Protraction of the US-Iran conflict does not serve the common interests of the parties concerned or the international community,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
He was responding to a question regarding Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's remarks to the ongoing 81st session of the UN General Assembly that Tehran will not allow freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz while sanctions and a US blockade remain in place, according to a transcript of Guo’s news conference.
“It is vital for parties to choose peace, resolve disputes through dialogue and negotiation, and restore peace and tranquility to the Middle East and Gulf region at an early date,” said Guo.
The statement from Beijing came as Xi is on a three-day state visit to the US, where he will hold summit-level talks with Trump.
Amid the ongoing US-Iran war, the Pentagon has imposed a military blockade of Iranian ports while Tehran has closed Hormuz, hitting global energy supplies.
"In waters in the Strait of Hormuz, ... we cannot let some have free access and gain their interests from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways," Pezeshkian told the General Assembly Wednesday.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 11 Chinese ships, 2 military aircraft
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked two Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and five official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Thursday and 6 a.m. on Friday.
One of the two People’s Liberation Army aircraft entered the country’s eastern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, the MND has tracked Chinese aircraft 210 times and ships 258 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: What Peacemaking Loses When Women Are Left Out
articles.body:
Wars exact a heavy toll on women and yet, too often their voices and concerns are pushed to the margins of global peacemaking. Since the end of the Cold War, the United Nations has made halting but real progress in bringing women into peace negotiations and postwar reconstruction from Guatemala to Bangsamoro and beyond.
Now that progress is being reversed. As peacemaking organizations fracture and lose their ability to press warring groups toward compromise, an assortment of social conservatives and warlords is finding new ways to exclude women from discussions about war and peace. Finding space for gender diversity could do more than ensure that women are heard; it could also give peace efforts a better chance of success.
About a decade ago, Colombia’s peace process culminated in an agreement that seemed to offer a lesson in how to end a deeply rooted conflict. Negotiators brought in the belligerents but they also consulted civil society groups on rural reform, inclusive governance, and accountability for wartime atrocities, including sexual violence. Women’s groups had a voice in these discussions.
The process had its shortcomings. Civil society was unevenly represented, and many of the peace agreement’s provisions on gender have yet to be fully carried out. Still, it rested on the premise that people with local relationships, legitimacy, and knowledge should be engaged in the peace process to help shape an enduring agreement.
That conviction is fading. Women are increasingly absent from the negotiating table. Recent diplomatic efforts—from Sudan’s peace talks, trade negotiations with China, Gaza’s Board of Peace—have featured teams composed entirely of men. Women’s representation may still be a top priority for some governments in prominent contexts, such as the selection of the next United Nations secretary-general, but it has become less visible in the daily diplomatic practice of making peace.
Today’s narrow ceasefire agreements struggle to secure even minimal protections against sexual violence: none of the 13 ceasefire agreements reached in 2025 prohibited it. The loss is both practical and moral. In many conflicts, women have political networks that men do not. They can connect humanitarian actors with communities, and act as bridges and brokers who can link local leaders with national processes.
A combination of factors helps explain why diplomacy has become less inclusive. Stalemates on the battlefield have encouraged a minimalist approach to peacemaking: diplomats and envoys bring military and political leaders together to stop the fighting, with less attention to conditions that would sustain peace.
As conflicts and postwar transitions grow more complex, diplomats have less room to pursue longer term goals such as political representation. Finally, diversity has become a point of contention. The Trump Administration has challenged efforts to increase representation of historically marginalized groups.
No countries for women
Sudan’s bloody war has raged for more than three years, and the need for an armistice is urgent. In September 2025, the United States, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, who are leading mediation efforts, proposed a humanitarian truce. The effort failed. Other diplomatic initiatives have tried to bring civilians into the conversation. An April conference in Berlin included women’s groups and other organizations, but it failed to persuade the warring parties to engage with anyone, much less with civil society. For now, even progress toward a basic ceasefire seems unattainable, making a broader approach to ending the violence ever more distant.
Diplomats with involvement and knowledge of the Sudan talks describe gender as a “non-starter” with the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces. Both factions have an interest in avoiding accountability for sexual violence and other atrocities while remaining focused on retaining their power. As Sudanese communities endure the war, diplomats are pursuing a narrow but pragmatic goal: finding a path to ceasefire while preserving space for later talks on who will have a voice in Sudan’s political future.
Elsewhere too, hopes for fair representation even in a postwar future remain bleak. Diversity is slipping off the diplomatic agenda in postwar Syria. Immediate concerns over stabilization and security takes precedence over any discussions of women’s representation between influential foreign governments and President Ahmad Al-Sharaa’s administration.
It remains unclear whether President al-Sharaa intends to build a government that reflects Syria’s diversity among women and men, and across its many ethnic and religious communities. Women hold just 22 of the recently formed parliament’s 207 seats. That number falls below the 20% quota for women in the electoral bodies from which the candidates were selected, and well short of the 30% target that civil society groups and the United Nations have often urged to increase political representation of women in Syria and elsewhere.
Across Syria, women hold meaningful influence in local community life. Parliamentarians might earn some communities’ trust over time, but women’s absence from national politics leaves a gap that a more inclusive system would be better equipped to close.
The manicured avenues of Washington are now home to some of the most powerful forces opposing diversity and gender justice. Even before the Trump Administration cast itself as a global peacemaker, its overwhelmingly male leadership had made opposition to diversity a defining feature of its foreign policy, rejecting the idea that a group can be considered oppressed based primarily on characteristics such as sex, race, or religion.
In its diplomacy at the United Nations and elsewhere, the Administration has made clear its opposition to quotas and other goals for representation. Senior U.S. officials have portrayed diversity as a weakness and linked traditional markers of masculinity, such as testosterone levels, to the ability to effectively deter battlefield threats.
The result is a vision of global power that places men at its center. Given Washington’s prominent role in many ongoing peace efforts, and Trump’s apparent affinity for strongmen, that stance reinforces the other two trends of minimalist peacemaking with a narrow set of elite interlocutors and an equally narrow set of issues to discuss. Some governments hesitate to raise diversity issues with the Trump Administration for fear of retaliation. Others, once more guarded in their opposition to diversity, now feel validated.
What communities can teach diplomats
Diversity may be losing ground in elite diplomacy, but it remains vital closer to the ground. Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms offer an example. When war broke out in April 2023, women who had worked in political resistance committees began organizing around their communities’ most urgent needs: protection, health care and psychosocial support.
They established Women’s Response Rooms to carry that work forward, drawing on networks built through years of efforts to claim a voice in public decisions. Across the wider network of Emergency Response Rooms, volunteers have negotiated humanitarian access, while women have mediated local disputes and helped hold communities together through conflict and displacement.
This extraordinary work takes place largely outside formal peace talks. Those peace processes may have changed, perhaps irreversibly, but local peacemaking persists. High-level negotiators should remember a lesson they once seemed to understand: Peace must be made not only by and for the belligerents in a conflict but also with and by people who have the legitimacy and relationships necessary to sustain societies through war and into peace.
The question now is whether diplomats will stay connected to those efforts and recognize what a peace process loses when it leaves the people sustaining their communities outside the room.

articles.title: Zelenskyy adviser denies agreement with Seoul to keep transfer of North Korean POWs secret
articles.body:
Zelenskyy adviser denies agreement with Seoul to keep transfer of North Korean POWs secret
Dmytro Lytvyn, communications adviser to the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied that Ukraine breached any agreement with South Korea not to disclose information about the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war.
Source: Lytvyn's comment in response to a post by Oksana Torop, media adviser to Ukraine's Ambassador to the UK Valerii Zaluzhnyi
Details: Torop wrote that Zelenskyy went to New York and publicly announced the transfer of the POWs to South Korea. "But there is a catch – an agreement between the countries and a non-disclosure agreement… And yet we know about it. A show, hype, a striking effect for a striking picture. Here we go…," she wrote.
Lytvyn replied under the post that this was not true. "There was no such agreement. That is false. And it would be wrong to conceal where particular prisoners are being sent," he said.
Previously: Earlier, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said that Ukraine had breached a non-disclosure agreement by publicly revealing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, and that making the information public could lead to numerous problems.
Background:
- In 2025, the Ukrainian military captured two North Korean soldiers in Russia's Kursk Oblast.
- It later emerged that a fake military ID discovered on a captured North Korean soldier in Kursk Oblast had been issued in the name of a real person from the Russian Republic of Tyva (Tuva).
- During his address to the UN General Assembly on 23 September, Zelenskyy said Ukraine recently transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
- He also said that one of the North Korean soldiers had tried to take his own life after realising he had been captured, saying this reflected the way people are indoctrinated in North Korea.
- Zelenskyy also addressed representatives of 47 countries whose citizens Russia is using in its war against Ukraine, urging them to look after their nationals and prevent Russia from drawing them into the war and sending them to fight on a foreign front.

articles.title: Russia, China, India responsible for keeping energy markets stable — senior diplomat
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Russia, China, and India bear a special responsibility for stability in global energy markets and the world at large, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko said in an interview with TASS.
"I am convinced that Russia, India, and China carry a special responsibility for solving key issues of global politics, including building a multipolar world order, strengthening a transparent and non-discriminatory trading system, and ensuring the stable and balanced development of food and energy markets," the Russian diplomat told TASS.
"These topics are regularly discussed at the leadership and ministerial levels within such formats as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), the core of which is essentially formed by the Russia-India-China trio," Rudenko noted.
"Coordinated approaches of our countries to international security issues, including the situation around Iran, were reflected in the Bishkek Declaration of the SCO Council of Heads of States," the deputy minister said. "Owing to close trilateral cooperation within BRICS, mutually acceptable language was managed to be found on Middle Eastern issues also, ensuring through that the adoption of the final document of the recent summit in New Delhi," Rudenko added.

articles.title: Satellite Imagery Reveals Damage at Russia’s Kuibyshev Oil Refinery Following Ukrainian Drone Strike
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Satellite Imagery Reveals Damage at Russia’s Kuibyshev Oil Refinery Following Ukrainian Drone Strike
Following a recent Ukrainian drone attack that sparked massive fires at the Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Russia’s Samara region, new satellite imagery has revealed the specific damage that forced the facility to suspend operations, the OSINT project “Absolutely Reliable Source” reported on September 25.
The new visual evidence follows the overnight attack on September 22, when Ukrainian drones struck the Rosneft-operated facility in retaliation for Russian strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, triggering explosions and massive fires. The Kuibyshev plant is one of the leading refineries in the Volga region, with an annual design capacity of 7 million tons of crude oil.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the “Absolutely Reliable Source,” the drone strike hit the refinery’s oil tank farm. The visual analysis confirmed that three storage tanks were destroyed by fire, with a fourth tank likely sustaining damage.
Additionally, the OSINT assessment identified a “scorched” pumping station and confirmed structural damage to the critical pipelines feeding the facility’s primary crude distillation units, designated as AVT-4 and AVT-5.
While the satellite imagery showed no signs of direct strikes or damage on the primary or secondary processing units themselves, the destruction of the supply infrastructure has effectively paralyzed the plant, the “Absolutely Reliable Source” wrote.
Based on the available information, the OSINT project noted that the refinery has completely halted operations, observing that it is nearly impossible for the distillation units to function without a stable supply of raw materials.
Ukrainian drones have also recently targeted Russia’s Rostov and Krasnodar regions overnight on September 24, striking facilities linked to oil storage. In the Rostov region, falling drone debris damaged administrative buildings at an oil depot in the Kagalnitsky district, though Governor Yury Slyusar reported no fire or casualties.
Meanwhile, in the Krasnodar region, a drone-induced fire broke out at an industrial facility identified by monitors as an oil depot in the village of Novotitarovskaya. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted a total of 40 Ukrainian drones across multiple regions and occupied Crimea during the nighttime barrage.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy broke confidentiality over North Korean POW disclosure: South Korea's Lee
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy broke a confidentiality agreement by disclosing that Ukraine had sent North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Seoul's president has said.
Thursday’s remarks by President Lee Jae-myung came after Zelenskyy told the United Nations that Ukraine had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, adding they were "not easy to capture alive".
The revelation prompted South Korea's political opposition to criticise the Lee administration for allowing a foreign leader to inform them of the prisoners' arrivals.
"I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," Lee said on X.
"The issue of bringing North Korean prisoners to South Korea is a highly sensitive one that could have a major impact on diplomacy, security and the situation on the Korean Peninsula," he said.
Confidentiality dispute
Lee said there had been calls to disclose the arrivals, but "given the problems that could arise from making it public, we agreed that keeping it confidential was the right thing to do".
Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn told journalists that Ukraine was "an open country" and that it would have been strange to hand over the soldiers in secret.
"From the entire story - which is long and detailed - we reported only the fact itself, that they were sent to the Republic of Korea," he said.
Early last year, Ukraine captured two North Korean soldiers among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow.
A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South.
Under South Korea's constitution, all Koreans, including those living in the North, are considered citizens, and officials have said this would apply to any North Korean troops captured in Ukraine.

articles.title: Israeli settlers deploy drones to abuse West Bank's Palestinians
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli settlers are using drones to forcibly change Palestinian life in the occupied West Bank
Rabie Abu Na’im vividly remembers the sound of the drone that Israeli settlers would launch daily over the Al-Khalayel Bedouin community east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank to monitor residents and eventually drive them out.
This community, which settlers succeeded in emptying following a relentless wave of attacks, was one of the areas where drones played a critical role in terrorising the Palestinian population and forcing them to flee.
Since the election of the Israeli government in 2022, settlers have employed various tactics in their declared campaign to seize land in the occupied West Bank, expand settlements, and densely establish outposts between Palestinian villages and towns to redraw territorial boundaries.
Among these tactics, drones have emerged as a key tool for the round-the-clock surveillance, intimidation, and expulsion of Palestinians, particularly herders, whom the drones pursue and force to retreat while they graze their livestock.
Recent reports indicate that Israeli settlement councils have also begun distributing drones to settlers for use in photography, reconnaissance, and monitoring the areas surrounding settlement outposts.
Abu Na’im told The New Arab that drones played a major role in the forced displacement of his community; over three years, Israeli settlers launched them to track residents' movements, with the drones becoming increasingly aggressive over time.
"When herders left their homes in the morning, the drones would pursue and shadow them; if they approached certain areas, settlers would gather to attack and drive them away. Eventually, the drones began monitoring residents inside their homes around the clock, and there was nothing anyone could do to stop them," he added.
Later, Israeli settlers began equipping drones with audio devices that broadcast insults and threats to Palestinians, warning them to leave the area. Women and children were terrified, and gradually residents left, coinciding with fierce physical assaults that injured many of them.
Drones were also frequently used to drop tear gas canisters on the communities targeted by settlers.
"A few days ago, when a boy and a young man were killed in Al-Mughayyir, drones played a major role. The raid began when a drone tracked a flock of sheep; settlers then attacked the site to steal the livestock under the protection of the Israeli army, which killed the two victims in cold blood during the incident," Rabie remarked.
Killer-bots in the sky
Drones can monitor vast areas, track the movement of people and livestock, and film Palestinian farmers and herders without settlers needing to approach them. Consequently, access to the land becomes exposed and monitored even before any direct confrontation occurs.
The situation is particularly dangerous for herding communities which rely on daily movement between their homes, grazing grounds, and water sources; areas that are increasingly encroached upon by rapidly expanding settlement outposts.
When the movements of herders are monitored from the air, settlers can pinpoint the location of livestock, determine when residents leave their homes and which areas they utilize, and then intervene to block their access to those lands.
Notably, this use of technology predates the recent distribution of equipment by years. Israeli funding had previously been revealed for equipping settlement outposts with gear, including drones, as part of a security package designed to monitor the surrounding areas.
However, Palestinians are convinced that its role goes far beyond that, as it has played a part in the killing of several boys and young men.
Mohammed Abu Siyam, a shepherd from the village of Mikhmas, east of Ramallah, recounted to TNA that Israeli settlers attacked the village last February and stole a herd of livestock; some Palestinians confronted them.
His son, Nasrallah, 19, was among the group and suggested climbing the mountain peak to locate the stolen herd. At that moment, the settlers launched a drone to track them.
“Using the drone, the settlers monitored my son and the others. An armed group of them lay in wait for the youths' arrival and immediately opened fire, killing Nasrallah and wounding other young men," he added.
To this day, the drone shadows Mohammed while he grazes his sheep, as if counting his livestock and inspecting everything with him, he said.
Off-limits to Palestinians
For Palestinian residents, the drone's very presence in the sky alters people's behavior.
A shepherd aware that his movements are being watched might hesitate to approach his own land; a farmer might avoid a specific area; and a family might reconsider staying in a place where every movement is subject to surveillance.
Imad Al-Batta, from the village of Hajjah near Qalqilya, told TNA that drones are violating the privacy of homes by flying extremely close to them, so close that families feel the devices might fly right through their windows.
"We are under surveillance by settlers' drones around the clock; privacy is non-existent, and everyone feels constantly threatened. These drones have also guided several settler attacks on the village, one of which resulted in the death of a young man and the injury of five others just days ago," he explained.
Yet, while drones are distributed to Israeli settlers and used without any oversight, Palestinians are prohibited from owning them even for purely professional purposes.
The Israeli army has arrested numerous Palestinian photojournalists over the past three years on the grounds of possessing a drone for photography.
Photojournalist Abdul Rahman Hassan, from Bethlehem, told TNA that soldiers raided his home on 19 August, arrested him, and transported him to a nearby detention center.
He remained handcuffed there for hours before an Israeli police vehicle transferred him to another detention center in the "Beitar Illit" settlement, where he was interrogated for hours regarding his possession of a drone.
"I told them I had always used it without anyone stopping me, but the interrogator informed me of a military order in place since 2017 prohibiting Palestinians from possessing such devices”.
They then made him sign documents acknowledging possession of a drone, and threatened that if he was found with a drone again, he would face imprisonment for many years.
In dozens of instances, the Israeli army has raided toy shops across various occupied West Bank cities, confiscating all drones even those intended as toys for children, and warning shop owners against selling them under threat of arrest.
A tool for forced displacement
Last May, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) documented the use of drones by Israeli settlers to pursue residents of the Arab al-Mleihat community in the Al-Ma’arajat area.
This occurred amidst a series of attacks and violations that ultimately resulted in the community being emptied of its residents.
Salah al-Khawaja, the Central Region official for the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, told TNA that the use of drones by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank follows two simultaneous tracks: one linked to the Israeli army, and the other to settlers, settler organisations, and settlement outposts.
He explained that the Israeli army conducts campaigns in Palestinian areas to confiscate drones, citing the pretext that they are used to monitor settler attacks and violations against Palestinians, and this occurs alongside the provision of advanced drones to settler organisations and outposts, ostensibly to ensure "security" for the settlers.
“Potential uses for these drones include filming Palestinian vehicles and recording their license plates, which allows for tracking the owners and taking legal action against them," he said.
The use of drones against Bedouin communities can extend beyond monitoring movements to surveilling residents' private lives, including filming their homes and enclosed areas within the communities.
"These practices can create a state of constant pressure on Palestinian families, particularly in Bedouin communities, leading them to feel targeted and unsafe in their own localities; given the nature and culture of Palestinian society, this can become an additional factor driving families to leave the areas where they live," he concluded.

articles.title: Ethiopia faces return to war as fighting spreads
articles.body:
Ethiopia faces return to war as fighting spreads
Fighting has escalated between Ethiopian troops and Tigrayan forces, triggering the suspension of flights to the holy town of Lalibela amid fears of a return to full-scale war in the north of the country.
Ethiopia’s federal army said it repelled attacks in Amhara’s North Wollo Zone and killed 272 Tigrayan fighters and wounded 260 others in a counteroffensive. Northeast army commander Lieutenant General Assefa Chekol said fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and allied groups attempted to break through at several locations.
“The army is carrying out the crucial task of clearing the occupied zone of the enemy by conducting targeted counter-attacks from key military positions it holds,” Chekol said in a statement on Thursday.
The suspension of flights to Lalibela, home to UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches, came a day after TPLF-linked forces seized airports in Mekelle, Axum, and Shire. Ethiopian Airlines also halted flights to these three cities in Tigray.
The two sides give conflicting accounts of how the fighting began. On Wednesday, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed accused the TPLF of launching an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Amhara and Afar. Tigray’s regional authorities said their troops entered a “defensive battle” after federal forces attacked them with aircraft, drones, and artillery on Tuesday.
“We are in the situation of full-blown war now,” TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa told AFP on Thursday.
The TPLF dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018. A power struggle between his government and Tigray’s leaders erupted into war in November 2020. Eritrean troops and Amhara forces fought alongside the federal army against Tigrayan forces. Hundreds of thousands died before an African Union-mediated peace agreement was signed in 2022. The agreement ended the large-scale war, but disputes over territory, the return of displaced people, and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces remain unresolved.
In May, the TPLF restored Tigray’s prewar regional council and elected party leader Debretsion Gebremichael as president following a dispute over the region’s leadership.
The latest escalation follows Sunday’s announcement of an alliance between the TPLF and six other groups, including its former Amhara adversaries, seeking to remove Abiy’s government.
The African Union has condemned the violence, warning that “the formation of new political and military alliances” risks further destabilizing the region and “reversing the gains made to silencing the guns, since 2020.” It said the airport seizures and detention of federal personnel violate the 2022 peace agreement, asking AU mediator and former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo to reengage with the parties. The UN has called for civilian protection and humanitarian access.

articles.title: China gets F-35 parts containing sensitive US technology – Bloomberg
articles.body:
China gets F-35 parts containing sensitive US technology – Bloomberg
China has obtained potentially sensitive components from the F-35, the US military’s most advanced stealth fighter jet, after the parts were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while being shipped from Australia to the US, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people briefed on the incident.
The incident first reported by Politico last week occurred earlier this year, when a shipment of allegedly unserviceable F-35 parts from Australia that was bound for the US was inexplicably rerouted.
US shipping giant UPS was transporting an F-35 canopy and weapons-bay door from the Australian Air Force to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal, people familiar with the incident told Bloomberg. The two components, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, were coated with radar-absorbing material designed to enhance the aircraft’s stealth capabilities, according to two sources cited by the outlet.
One of the sources said the transport aircraft stopped in South Korea on its way to the US, after which the shipment was rerouted to Hong Kong. It remains unclear why the aircraft stopped there, why the shipment was sent to Hong Kong, or whether the rerouting was intentional or accidental, the source said. Two sources added that Chinese authorities subsequently seized the components, which have not been returned.
The F-35, one of the world’s most advanced fighter jets, is operated by around 20 countries, including South Korea, Japan, Singapore and Australia. Australia serves as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific for storing spare parts and maintaining F-35s operated by nearby US allies.
At least two congressional committees are investigating the latest incident, the news agency noted. Earlier this week, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles confirmed that Canberra was working with the US and Lockheed Martin to examine its role in the shipment blunder. Marles stressed that the missing components were not sensitive.
According to a Lockheed Martin spokesperson in Australia, “the components in question are unserviceable and deemed low risk for exploitation.”
The disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries, as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
China’s Foreign Ministry said it was not aware of the incident, while the Hong Kong government declined to comment on specific cases.

articles.title: Iran threatens to hit back at countries that ban its airlines
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran threatens to hit back at countries that ban its airlines
Iran's national security chief has threatened to hit back at countries that cooperate with US attempts to cripple its aviation industry as route cancellations gather pace.
A handful of countries have suspended Iran-operated flights in recent days after the Trump administration threatened to target them with sanctions if they continued to deal with Iranian airlines.
"If you stand by America, we will not simply watch you … your airports will have no flights," Mohsen Rezaei, the head of the Supreme National Security Council, said on state TV on Wednesday.
The US earlier this month imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airliners, including state-owned Iran Air and Mahan, Iran's largest carrier, as part of its efforts to crush the country's economy.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that any organisation that continues to work with airlines after 23 September would be frozen out of the dollar financial system. That includes any company that provides services, such as ground handling and ticketing, as well as airport operators.
Several countries have suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers since the announcement, including Turkey, Oman, Azerbaijan and Georgia.
The most recent was the United Arab Emirates, which Iranian media said on Thursday had cancelled all flights operated by Iranian airlines.
As of Thursday, Mahan was also no longer listing flights to India and Malaysia. Neither of the countries has officially announced that flights would be suspended.
A handful of countries have yet to comply with the sanctions, including China and Iraq.
Beijing has opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal under international law.
Iraq, among the top destination countries for Iranian travellers, has not officially announced that it would ban Iranian airlines, though anonymous government officials have said flights would be suspended. As of Thursday morning, Mahan was offering tickets to Najaf and Baghdad.
The airline is also continuing to list flights to Russia, Pakistan and Thailand.
International travel was already heavily restricted for Iranian passengers before the latest sanctions. Flights to key destinations in the region such as Turkey and the UAE had been curtailed by the war, and many major international carriers had suspended routes to Iran.

articles.title: Zelensky warns of drone shortages in winter due to $27B budget deficit
articles.body:
Zelensky warns of drone shortages in winter due to $27B budget deficit
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this while speaking to journalists, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"As for the $27 billion [defense budget deficit], of course, part of it covers payments to our soldiers, but overall, most of it is funding for our drones, missiles and support for our soldiers. There is October, November and December. But what is important is that about a third of this money, perhaps even slightly more, is for January, February and March – for drones. And if we do not place the orders and make the payments in October and November, we will face serious challenges in January and February, above all," Zelensky said.
According to him, he discussed the issue in detail with the European Union, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, as well as with the International Monetary Fund.
"The International Monetary Fund has nothing to do with military support, with drones – those are completely different issues. As for the European Commission, I am strongly asking it to bring forward the second tranche of the $90 billion, because, once again, January and February need to be supplied with the necessary drones and missiles," Zelensky said.

articles.title: Man appears in London court accused of providing Russian intelligence with drone factory details
articles.body:
Man appears in London court accused of providing Russian intelligence with drone factory details
LONDON, Sept 25 - A British man will go on trial next year accused of providing information about factories which manufacture drones and offering to sabotage them on behalf of Russian intelligence, a London court was told on Friday.
Joshua Cammidge, 31, is charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparing an act of sabotage after contact with the GRU Volunteer Corps, which prosecutors said was controlled by Russia's GRU military intelligence agency.
Prosecutor Sarah Przybylska told London's Old Bailey court that Cammidge, from Swindon, west England, had exchanged messages with a British national who had gone to Russia to fight against Ukraine, in which Cammidge was tasked with locating drone manufacturing sites.
"They discussed sabotaging a site and the defendant volunteered to carry out such sabotage," she said. "It was clear all of this was to assist the Russian war effort."
Prosecutors have also accused him of conducting research about a Wi-Fi jamming device and undertaking reconnaissance.
Cammidge was not asked to enter pleas, but his lawyer John Oliver told the court he intended to deny the accusations.
Oliver said there was "no intention to cause or take part in sabotage" and the communications between the men were "not to be taken seriously".
Russia's embassy in London has not commented on the case. Cammidge was remanded in custody and will appear again in court to enter a plea in January, with the trial due to take place at Winchester Crown Court in April. REUTERS
